In this page you run five such tests on one myasthenia gravis (MG) thymus section. A *spot* is one capture location of the spatial assay. A *clone* is a group of receptors that descend from one ancestor cell. | Question | Function | Statistic | |----|----|----| | Does one variable cluster in space? | `spatialMoran()` | Global Moran’s I | | Where are the clusters? | `spatialLocalMoran()` | Local Moran’s I | | Do two variables have the same spatial pattern? | `spatialLee()` | Lee’s L | | Are spots of type A near spots of type B? | `spatialRipleyCrossK()` | Ripley’s cross K | | Do the spots of one clone sit next to each other? | `spatialCloneJoinCount()` | Join count | `spatialCloneSpread()` adds a sixth measure. It reports how far each clone spreads across a section. For help with the choice of test, see [Choose a spatial statistic](choose-spatial-statistic.md). Each function accepts a SIRUP object. It reads the spot coordinates and the image settings from the object. ## Get the example data This page uses example files that are not part of the SIRUP package. This code downloads them. Change `dest` to a folder you want to keep. The default folder is temporary. The function skips files that are already there. ``` r extdata <- SIRUP::downloadSIRUPExample( dest = file.path(tempdir(), "SIRUP_example"), files = c( "mg_thymus_cell_types.csv.gz", "mg_thymus_slice2_bcr.tsv.gz", "mg_thymus_slice2_gc_polygons.csv", "mg_thymus_slice2_spatial.rds", "mg_thymus_slice2_tcr.tsv.gz" ) ) #> ℹ 'mg_thymus_cell_types.csv.gz' is already in '/tmp/RtmpWzQrg2/SIRUP_example'. #> ℹ 'mg_thymus_slice2_bcr.tsv.gz' is already in '/tmp/RtmpWzQrg2/SIRUP_example'. #> ℹ 'mg_thymus_slice2_gc_polygons.csv' is already in '/tmp/RtmpWzQrg2/SIRUP_example'. #> ℹ 'mg_thymus_slice2_spatial.rds' is already in '/tmp/RtmpWzQrg2/SIRUP_example'. #> ℹ 'mg_thymus_slice2_tcr.tsv.gz' is already in '/tmp/RtmpWzQrg2/SIRUP_example'. ``` ## Set up the object Load the packages, then build one SIRUP object with a BCR slot and a TCR slot from the example data. ``` r library(SIRUP) library(dplyr) library(ggplot2) ``` ``` r read_receptors <- function(file, locus) { airr::read_rearrangement(file.path(extdata, file)) %>% extractSpatialIds( id = "sequence_id", spatial_id = "barcode_10x", regex = ",([ACGT]{16})$", suffix = "-1" ) %>% filterAirr( locus_val = locus, min_v_length = 250, min_j_length = 30, min_junction_length = 10, productive_only = TRUE, min_consensus_count = NULL, spatial_id = "barcode_10x" ) %>% filter(!grepl("[^ACGT]", junction)) } thymus <- readRDS(file.path(extdata, "mg_thymus_slice2_spatial.rds")) cell_types <- data.table::fread( file.path(extdata, "mg_thymus_cell_types.csv.gz"), data.table = FALSE ) %>% filter(sample == "mg_thymus_slice2") rownames(cell_types) <- cell_types$barcode thymus <- Seurat::AddMetaData(thymus, select(cell_types, -sample, -barcode)) sirup <- createSIRUP( spatial = thymus, receptors = list( BCR = read_receptors("mg_thymus_slice2_bcr.tsv.gz", "IGH"), TCR = read_receptors("mg_thymus_slice2_tcr.tsv.gz", "TRB") ), spatial_id = "barcode_10x", image_scale = "lowres", swap_coords = FALSE, polygons_path = file.path(extdata, "mg_thymus_slice2_gc_polygons.csv") ) #> filterAirr kept 2189 of 3793 rows (dropped 1604). #> filterAirr kept 3718 of 7915 rows (dropped 4197). sirup <- updateReceptors( sirup, scoper::hierarchicalClones, slot = "BCR", threshold = 0.1, summarize_clones = FALSE, nproc = 1 ) #> Running defineClonesScoper in bulk mode and only keep heavy chains ``` `read_receptors()` reads a consensus table. It takes the spot barcode from `sequence_id`. It keeps the high-quality sequences of one locus that have an unambiguous junction. The object holds two receptor slots, `"BCR"` and `"TCR"`. Functions that read receptors take a `slot` argument. BCR clones come from `scoper::hierarchicalClones()`. The cell-type table holds the estimated proportion of each cell type in each spot. The proportions come from the cell2location method and join the Seurat metadata. The object also holds the polygons that mark the ectopic germinal centers (eGCs). [Draw tissue regions and measure clonal dominance and diversity](regions.md) explains polygons. ## Choose the neighbors Most of these statistics compare each spot with its neighbors. You choose the neighbors in one of two ways: - `k`: the `k` nearest spots. Use `k = 6` for standard Visium, where each spot has six neighbors on a hexagonal grid. Use `k = 8` for Visium HD, where each bin has eight neighbors on a square grid. A larger `k` measures patterns over larger distances. - `radius`: all spots within a distance. SIRUP measures distances in image pixels at the stored `image_scale`. The same distance in micrometers needs a different number at `"lowres"` and at `"hires"`.

Tip

`k` does not depend on the image scale. Use it as the default.
## Test one variable with global Moran’s I *Moran’s I* measures spatial autocorrelation. It asks whether neighboring spots have similar values. $$I = \frac{N}{W} \frac{\sum_i \sum_j w_{ij}(x_i - \bar{x})(x_j - \bar{x})}{\sum_i (x_i - \bar{x})^2}$$ Here $x_i$ is the value at spot $i$. $w_{ij}$ is 1 if spot $j$ is a neighbor of spot $i$, and 0 if not. $N$ is the number of spots. $W$ is the sum of all $w_{ij}$. $I$ near 0 means no spatial pattern. Positive $I$ means that similar values cluster. Negative $I$ means that values alternate, as on a chessboard. `variable_type` tells SIRUP what `variable` is: - `"feature"`: a gene, from the assay and layer you give. - `"metadata"`: a numeric spot metadata column. For a text column, give `value` to test the spots that have that value. - `"receptor"`: 1 for spots with any receptor and 0 for other spots. `variable` is a label only. - `"clone"`: 1 for spots with the clone that `variable` names. ``` r aicda <- spatialMoran( sirup, variable = "AICDA", variable_type = "feature", assay = "Spatial", layer = "data", k = 6 ) aicda$test #> #> Moran I test under randomisation #> #> data: dat$value #> weights: listw #> #> Moran I statistic standard deviate = 6.0618, p-value = 6.731e-10 #> alternative hypothesis: greater #> sample estimates: #> Moran I statistic Expectation Variance #> 5.944121e-02 -3.123048e-04 9.716874e-05 ``` The result is a list. `test` is the `spdep::moran.test()` result. It holds the statistic, its expected value under no spatial pattern, the variance, and the p value. For *AICDA* (a marker of germinal center B cells), $I$ is small, about 0.06. The p value is below $10^{-9}$. The assay detects *AICDA* in few spots, and most spots have a count of zero. The clustering is weak, but chance is a poor explanation for it. Read $I$ for the size of the pattern and the p value for the evidence. The same function tests cell-type proportions and receptor presence: ``` r moran_table <- bind_rows( tibble(variable = "AICDA expression", I = aicda$test$estimate[[1]], p = aicda$test$p.value), { res <- spatialMoran(sirup, variable = "GC B", variable_type = "metadata", k = 6) tibble(variable = "GC B cell proportion", I = res$test$estimate[[1]], p = res$test$p.value) }, { res <- spatialMoran(sirup, slot = "BCR", variable = "BCR", variable_type = "receptor", k = 6) tibble(variable = "BCR present", I = res$test$estimate[[1]], p = res$test$p.value) }, { res <- spatialMoran(sirup, slot = "TCR", variable = "TCR", variable_type = "receptor", k = 6) tibble(variable = "TCR present", I = res$test$estimate[[1]], p = res$test$p.value) } ) moran_table #> # A tibble: 4 × 3 #> variable I p #> #> 1 AICDA expression 0.0594 6.73e- 10 #> 2 GC B cell proportion 0.623 0 #> 3 BCR present 0.417 0 #> 4 TCR present 0.332 1.31e-238 ``` The GC B cell proportion has a stronger cluster, with $I$ near 0.62. The cell2location estimate is smooth and has no zeros from sampling. A p value of 0 means a value below the smallest number that R can store. Moran’s I accepts binary variables, such as receptor presence. The join-count test below suits clones better. ## Find clusters with local Moran’s I Global Moran’s I gives one number for the whole section. *Local Moran’s I* (also called LISA) gives one value for each spot. A spot has a high positive value when it and its neighbors have similar values. The z-score shows how far the value is from the value expected by chance. ``` r gc_b_local <- spatialLocalMoran( sirup, variable = "GC B", variable_type = "metadata", k = 6 ) head(gc_b_local[, c("cell", "value", "local_i", "z_i", "p_value")]) #> cell value local_i z_i p_value #> 1 AAACAAGTATCTCCCA-1 0.0556 0.42119564 1.8775350 0.060444809 #> 2 AAACACCAATAACTGC-1 0.0492 0.02554433 0.1780355 0.858695126 #> 3 AAACAGCTTTCAGAAG-1 0.0128 0.67548360 2.1434191 0.032079462 #> 4 AAACAGGGTCTATATT-1 0.0149 0.44557822 1.5436247 0.122679267 #> 5 AAACAGTGTTCCTGGG-1 0.0251 0.10316582 0.6444111 0.519308914 #> 6 AAACATGGTGAGAGGA-1 0.0915 2.05891309 3.0435870 0.002337758 ``` `plotSpatialLocalMoran()` draws the z-scores on the tissue. Red spots sit in clusters of similar values. Blue spots differ from their neighbors: ``` r plotSpatialLocalMoran( sirup, gc_b_local, point_size = 1, title = "GC B cell proportion, local Moran's I (z-score)" ) + guides(color = guide_colorbar(title = "z")) ``` ![](spatial-statistics_files/figure-gfm/local-moran-plot-1.jpeg) The clusters of high GC B cell proportion sit at the eGC polygons. Each spot has its own p value. Correct for multiple testing before you call a spot significant. For example, use `p.adjust(method = "BH")`. ## Compare two variables with Lee’s L *Lee’s L* combines Pearson correlation with spatial smoothing. It is high when two variables are high in the same neighborhoods. The variables need not peak in the same spots. In MG, patients make antibodies against the acetylcholine receptor (AChR). *CHRNA1* codes for the AChR alpha subunit, and thymic myoid cells express it. This test asks whether *CHRNA1* and the germinal center marker *AICDA* share a spatial pattern. *MS4A1* (CD20) gives a positive control, because GC B cells express both *MS4A1* and *AICDA*: ``` r lee_control <- spatialLee( sirup, x = "AICDA", y = "MS4A1", assay = "Spatial", layer = "data", k = 6 ) lee_chrna1 <- spatialLee( sirup, x = "AICDA", y = "CHRNA1", assay = "Spatial", layer = "data", k = 6 ) tibble( pair = c("AICDA and MS4A1", "AICDA and CHRNA1"), L = c(lee_control$L, lee_chrna1$L), p = c(lee_control$test$p.value, lee_chrna1$test$p.value) ) #> # A tibble: 2 × 3 #> pair L p #> #> 1 AICDA and MS4A1 0.0975 2.17e-49 #> 2 AICDA and CHRNA1 -0.00171 5.66e- 1 ``` The control pair shares a pattern. *AICDA* and *CHRNA1* do not. In this section, $L$ for that pair is near zero and the test is not significant.

Warning

The analytical test (`method = "analytical"`) builds a dense matrix with one entry for each pair of spots. This works for Visium. For Visium HD, use `method = "mc"`. It uses permutations and sparse weights.
## Test two spot types with Ripley’s cross K *Ripley’s cross K* counts, for each distance $r$, how many type B points lie within $r$ of an average type A point: $$K_{AB}(r) = \frac{|W|}{N_A N_B} \sum_{i \in A} \sum_{j \in B} \mathbf{1}(d_{ij} \le r)$$ $|W|$ is the area of the tissue window. $d_{ij}$ is the distance between points $i$ and $j$. SIRUP compares the observed curve with curves from random relabeling of the points. If the observed curve is above the envelope of the random curves, A and B sit closer than chance. T follicular helper (Tfh) cells give B cells the signals that keep a germinal center going. This test asks whether spots with GC B cells sit near spots with Tfh cells. First, label each spot from its cell2location proportions. `updateSpatial()` runs a function on the Seurat object and stores the result: ``` r sirup <- updateSpatial(sirup, function(spatial) { gc_b <- spatial$`GC B` > 0.10 tfh <- spatial$Tfh > 0.10 spatial$gc_tfh_mark <- case_when( gc_b & !tfh ~ "GC B", tfh & !gc_b ~ "Tfh", TRUE ~ NA_character_ ) spatial }) table(getSpatial(sirup)$gc_tfh_mark, useNA = "ifany") #> #> GC B Tfh #> 76 211 2916 ``` Spots with neither cell type, or with both, get `NA`. The test leaves them out. Then run the test. `nsim` sets the number of random relabelings. Use 99 or more for a final analysis: ``` r gc_tfh_k <- spatialRipleyCrossK( sirup, mark_col = "gc_tfh_mark", i = "GC B", j = "Tfh", nsim = 39, max_r = 40 ) plotRipleyCrossK(gc_tfh_k, title = "Cross K: GC B spots to Tfh spots") ``` ![](spatial-statistics_files/figure-gfm/ripley-1.jpeg) The distance $r$ is in image pixels at the stored `image_scale`. To convert it to micrometers, use the Visium spot size. A spot is 55 µm wide. The image object stores the spot diameter in full-resolution pixels: ``` r scale_factors <- getSpatial(sirup)@images[[1]]@scale.factors um_per_pixel <- 55 / (scale_factors$spot * scale_factors$lowres) um_per_pixel #> [1] 11.7135 max(gc_tfh_k$plot_data$r) * um_per_pixel #> [1] 468.5401 ``` The value `max_r = 40` lowres pixels is about 470 µm. In this section, the observed curve lies below the envelope at every distance. Random relabeling keeps the marked spots in place and shuffles the labels. A curve below the envelope means that GC B spots sit next to other GC B spots more often than next to Tfh spots. The same holds for Tfh spots. The two cell types form separate groups at the 10% threshold. The rule that drops spots with both cell types adds to the separation. Change the thresholds or the marks to ask a different question. ## Test whether a clone stays together with join counts The join-count test suits a clone. Take every spot with a BCR. Mark the spots that have the clone. Count the neighbor pairs in which both spots have the clone. Each pair is a “join”. If the clone stays in one place, the section has more joins than random labeling gives. `spatialCloneJoinCount()` runs `spdep::joincount.test()` for each clone that occurs in at least `min_spatial_ids` spots. If the object has stored polygons, the function runs one test for each polygon by default. Set `use_stored_polygons = FALSE` for one test over the whole section: ``` r big_clones <- getReceptors(sirup, slot = "BCR") %>% filter(!is.na(barcode_10x)) %>% distinct(clone_id, barcode_10x) %>% count(clone_id, sort = TRUE) %>% slice_head(n = 5) %>% pull(clone_id) join_count <- spatialCloneJoinCount( sirup, slot = "BCR", clone_val = big_clones, use_stored_polygons = FALSE, k = 6, return_data = TRUE ) join_count$summary #> clone_id image polygon n_spatial_ids n_clone_spatial_ids #> 1 598 thymus_slice2 all 797 11 #> 2 288 thymus_slice2 all 797 27 #> 3 34 thymus_slice2 all 797 66 #> 4 64 thymus_slice2 all 797 10 #> 5 196 thymus_slice2 all 797 27 #> observed_join_count expected_join_count variance statistic p_value #> 1 12.5 0.4145729 0.3644266 20.019673 1.855757e-89 #> 2 30.0 2.6457286 2.2476408 18.245749 1.118248e-74 #> 3 67.5 16.1683417 12.6054484 14.457931 1.117067e-47 #> 4 5.5 0.3391960 0.2987982 9.441226 1.842208e-21 #> 5 15.5 2.6457286 2.2476408 8.574011 4.997114e-18 #> method radius k alternative #> 1 Join count test under nonfree sampling NA 6 greater #> 2 Join count test under nonfree sampling NA 6 greater #> 3 Join count test under nonfree sampling NA 6 greater #> 4 Join count test under nonfree sampling NA 6 greater #> 5 Join count test under nonfree sampling NA 6 greater ``` The summary has one row for each clone. `statistic` is the standardized join count (a z-score). `p_value` is the one-sided p value. `plotSpatialCloneJoinCount()` shows the clone and its joins. The plot needs `return_data = TRUE` in the test: ``` r plotSpatialCloneJoinCount( join_count = join_count, object = sirup, clone_val = join_count$summary$clone_id[[1]], show_neighbors = TRUE ) ``` ![](spatial-statistics_files/figure-gfm/join-count-plot-1.jpeg) ## Measure how far a clone spreads `spatialCloneSpread()` describes how far each clone reaches across the section. It uses the pairwise distances between the sequences of the clone: ``` r spread <- spatialCloneSpread(sirup, slot = "BCR", min_spatial_ids = 3) spread %>% arrange(desc(n_spatial_ids)) %>% head() #> # A tibble: 6 × 5 #> sample clone_id n_spatial_ids mean_pairwise_distance max_pairwise_distance #> #> 1 spatial 34 86 66.2 397. #> 2 spatial 288 42 123. 304. #> 3 spatial 196 38 156. 395. #> 4 spatial 739 16 21.5 75.1 #> 5 spatial 810 14 80.0 263. #> 6 spatial 907 14 54.2 120. ``` The table gives the mean and the maximum pairwise distance for each clone, in image pixels. By default, sequences in the same spot count as separate points at distance 0. Set `collapse_within_spot = TRUE` to count each spot once. ## Keep the results Store the results in the object, so they travel with the data: ``` r sirup <- sirup %>% setAnalysis("moran_aicda", aicda) %>% setAnalysis("local_moran_gc_b", gc_b_local) %>% setAnalysis("lee_aicda_chrna1", lee_chrna1) %>% setAnalysis("clone_join_count", join_count) %>% setAnalysis("clone_spread", spread) listAnalyses(sirup) #> [1] "moran_aicda" "local_moran_gc_b" "lee_aicda_chrna1" "clone_join_count" #> [5] "clone_spread" ``` ## Next steps - Pick a test from your question: [Choose a spatial statistic](choose-spatial-statistic.md). - Draw regions and compare their repertoires: [Draw tissue regions and measure clonal dominance and diversity](regions.md). - Build lineage trees for the clones that you found: [Call clones and build lineage trees on the tissue](clones-and-trees.md). - Run the tests on several sections: [Analyze several sections with bulk AIRR-seq and blood](multisample.md).

pages.title: Analyze several sections with bulk AIRR-seq and blood
pages.summary: Put several tissue sections, bulk AIRR-seq, and blood samples in one SIRUP object, and follow clones between them.
pages.markdown:
Analyze several sections with bulk AIRR-seq and blood ================

Note

**Time:** ~25 minutes.
**Data:** two MG thymus sections, bulk thymus BCR-seq, and bulk blood BCR-seq, downloaded with `downloadSIRUPExample()`.
**Needs:** SIRUP, scoper, and dowser. The tree step also needs the IMGT reference sequences.
Most studies have more than one tissue section. You can also have bulk AIRR-seq of the same tissue, or blood from other time points. In this page, you put all of these samples in one SIRUP object. You call clones on all samples together. You then ask where each clone was seen, compare clonal dominance in each section, and build a lineage tree that has blood tips. A clone is a group of B or T cells that descend from one ancestor cell and share its receptor rearrangement. If you call clones on all samples together, one clone ID names the same lineage in every sample. One SIRUP object can hold all of this: - `spatial` can be a named list of Seurat objects, one for each section. - The receptor table holds the rows from every section and every bulk sample. A `sample` column tells SIRUP which sample each row belongs to. - Rows whose `sample` does not name a section stay in the table as nonspatial rows. SIRUP does not put them on a tissue. Clone calling, trees, and your own summaries can use them. This page follows Figure 5 of the SIRUP paper. The MG thymus data come from a patient who had a thymectomy. Besides the two Visium sections, there is bulk BCR-seq of the thymus. There is also bulk BCR-seq of blood, taken at the thymectomy and 12 months later. The question is which clones in ectopic germinal centers (eGCs) also appear in the blood. An eGC is a site in the thymus where B cells proliferate and mutate their receptors. ## Get the example data This page uses example files that are not part of the SIRUP package. This code downloads them. Change `dest` to a folder you want to keep. The default folder is temporary. The function skips files that are already there. ``` r extdata <- SIRUP::downloadSIRUPExample( dest = file.path(tempdir(), "SIRUP_example"), files = c( "mg_thymus_slice1_spatial.rds", "mg_thymus_slice2_spatial.rds", "mg_thymus_slice1_bcr.tsv.gz", "mg_thymus_slice2_bcr.tsv.gz", "mg_thymus_slice2_tcr.tsv.gz", "mg_thymus_slice1_gc_polygons.csv", "mg_thymus_slice2_gc_polygons.csv", "mg_thymus_bulk_thymus_1.tsv.gz", "mg_thymus_bulk_thymus_2.tsv.gz", "mg_thymus_bulk_blood_month0_1.tsv.gz", "mg_thymus_bulk_blood_month0_2.tsv.gz", "mg_thymus_bulk_blood_month12_1.tsv.gz", "mg_thymus_bulk_blood_month12_2.tsv.gz" ) ) #> ℹ Downloading 'mg_thymus_slice1_spatial.rds' #> ℹ 'mg_thymus_slice2_spatial.rds' is already in '/tmp/RtmpWzQrg2/SIRUP_example'. #> ℹ Downloading 'mg_thymus_slice1_bcr.tsv.gz' #> ℹ 'mg_thymus_slice2_bcr.tsv.gz' is already in '/tmp/RtmpWzQrg2/SIRUP_example'. #> ℹ 'mg_thymus_slice2_tcr.tsv.gz' is already in '/tmp/RtmpWzQrg2/SIRUP_example'. #> ℹ Downloading 'mg_thymus_slice1_gc_polygons.csv' #> ℹ 'mg_thymus_slice2_gc_polygons.csv' is already in '/tmp/RtmpWzQrg2/SIRUP_example'. #> ℹ Downloading 'mg_thymus_bulk_thymus_1.tsv.gz' #> ℹ Downloading 'mg_thymus_bulk_thymus_2.tsv.gz' #> ℹ Downloading 'mg_thymus_bulk_blood_month0_1.tsv.gz' #> ℹ Downloading 'mg_thymus_bulk_blood_month0_2.tsv.gz' #> ℹ Downloading 'mg_thymus_bulk_blood_month12_1.tsv.gz' #> ℹ Downloading 'mg_thymus_bulk_blood_month12_2.tsv.gz' ``` ## Load the samples ``` r library(SIRUP) library(dplyr) library(ggplot2) ``` ``` r spatial <- list( mg_thymus_slice1 = readRDS(file.path(extdata, "mg_thymus_slice1_spatial.rds")), mg_thymus_slice2 = readRDS(file.path(extdata, "mg_thymus_slice2_spatial.rds")) ) read_bcrs <- function(file, sample, compartment) { airr::read_rearrangement(file.path(extdata, file)) %>% mutate(sample = sample, compartment = compartment) } sections <- bind_rows( read_bcrs("mg_thymus_slice1_bcr.tsv.gz", "mg_thymus_slice1", "thymus_slice1"), read_bcrs("mg_thymus_slice2_bcr.tsv.gz", "mg_thymus_slice2", "thymus_slice2") ) %>% extractSpatialIds( id = "sequence_id", spatial_id = "barcode_10x", regex = ",([ACGT]{16})$", suffix = "-1" ) bulk <- bind_rows( read_bcrs("mg_thymus_bulk_thymus_1.tsv.gz", "bulk_thymus_1", "bulk_thymus"), read_bcrs("mg_thymus_bulk_thymus_2.tsv.gz", "bulk_thymus_2", "bulk_thymus"), read_bcrs("mg_thymus_bulk_blood_month0_1.tsv.gz", "bulk_blood_month0_1", "blood_month0"), read_bcrs("mg_thymus_bulk_blood_month0_2.tsv.gz", "bulk_blood_month0_2", "blood_month0"), read_bcrs("mg_thymus_bulk_blood_month12_1.tsv.gz", "bulk_blood_month12_1", "blood_month12"), read_bcrs("mg_thymus_bulk_blood_month12_2.tsv.gz", "bulk_blood_month12_2", "blood_month12") ) bcrs <- bind_rows(sections, bulk) %>% mutate(sequence_id = paste(sample, gsub(",", "_", sequence_id), sep = "_")) %>% filterAirr( locus_val = "IGH", min_v_length = 250, min_j_length = 30, min_junction_length = 10, productive_only = TRUE, min_consensus_count = NULL ) %>% filter(!grepl("[^ACGT]", junction)) #> filterAirr kept 5733 of 8849 rows (dropped 3116). count(bcrs, compartment, sample) #> # A tibble: 8 × 3 #> compartment sample n #> #> 1 blood_month0 bulk_blood_month0_1 182 #> 2 blood_month0 bulk_blood_month0_2 182 #> 3 blood_month12 bulk_blood_month12_1 241 #> 4 blood_month12 bulk_blood_month12_2 108 #> 5 bulk_thymus bulk_thymus_1 176 #> 6 bulk_thymus bulk_thymus_2 576 #> 7 thymus_slice1 mg_thymus_slice1 1967 #> 8 thymus_slice2 mg_thymus_slice2 2105 tcrs <- read_bcrs("mg_thymus_slice2_tcr.tsv.gz", "mg_thymus_slice2", "thymus_slice2") %>% extractSpatialIds( id = "sequence_id", spatial_id = "barcode_10x", regex = ",([ACGT]{16})$", suffix = "-1" ) %>% mutate(sequence_id = paste(sample, gsub(",", "_", sequence_id), sep = "_")) %>% filterAirr( locus_val = "TRB", min_v_length = 250, min_j_length = 30, min_junction_length = 10, productive_only = TRUE, min_consensus_count = NULL ) %>% filter(!grepl("[^ACGT]", junction)) #> filterAirr kept 3718 of 7915 rows (dropped 4197). ``` `read_bcrs()` reads one AIRR file (BCRs or TCRs) and adds two columns: `sample` and `compartment`. After the barcodes come out of the section IDs, the code makes each `sequence_id` unique and safe for trees. It puts the sample name in front, because IDs repeat between files. It replaces the comma with `_`, because dowser renames tree tips that contain a comma. The section rows get a `sample` that matches the names of the `spatial` list. The bulk and blood rows have their own sample names and no barcode.

Note

To keep the package small, the bulk files hold a subset of the bulk data. They hold the blood sequences of clones seen in a section. They also hold up to 10 bulk thymus sequences of each clone that reaches the blood.
## Create a multi-sample object Give `createSIRUP()` the named list of Seurat objects. Give `receptors` a named list of receptor tables. The tables are the slots `"BCR"` and `"TCR"`. Only section 2 has TCRs. Give the name of the `sample` column to `sample_id`. All slots use this column. ``` r sirup <- createSIRUP( spatial = spatial, receptors = list(BCR = bcrs, TCR = tcrs), spatial_id = "barcode_10x", sample_id = "sample", image_scale = "lowres", swap_coords = FALSE ) sirup #> #> Spatial data: Seurat, 6,599 spatial IDs, 449 genes, 2 spatial samples, 2 images #> Receptor data: 2 slots #> BCR: 5,537 receptor sequences x 58 columns; 1,567/1,640 receptor IDs in spatial data (95.5%) #> TCR: 3,610 receptor sequences x 58 columns; 1,414/1,571 receptor IDs in spatial data (90.0%) #> Samples: 2 #> Spatial ID field: barcode_10x #> Sample ID field: sample #> Analyses: 0 spatialSamples(sirup) #> [1] "mg_thymus_slice1" "mg_thymus_slice2" ``` Visium barcodes repeat between sections. For example, `AAACAAGTATCTCCCA-1` exists in both. SIRUP matches each receptor to a spot by the pair of sample and barcode, so the two sections never mix. A spot is one capture area of the Visium slide. If the sections need different image settings, give named values: `image_scale = c(mg_thymus_slice1 = "hires", mg_thymus_slice2 = "lowres")`. ## Get one sample The accessors take a `sample_id` argument. The receptor accessors also take a `slot` argument. ``` r getSpatial(sirup, "mg_thymus_slice1") #> An object of class Seurat #> 506 features across 3396 samples within 2 assays #> Active assay: Spatial (449 features, 0 variable features) #> 2 layers present: counts, data #> 1 other assay present: alra #> 1 spatial field of view present: thymus_slice1 nrow(getReceptors(sirup, "mg_thymus_slice1", slot = "BCR")) #> [1] 1967 nrow(getReceptors(sirup, slot = "BCR")) #> [1] 5537 ``` `filterSample()` returns a new SIRUP object with one section. It drops the nonspatial rows. ``` r slice1 <- filterSample(sirup, "mg_thymus_slice1") slice1 #> #> Spatial data: Seurat, 3,396 spatial IDs, 449 genes, 1 image #> Receptor data: 2 slots #> BCR: 1,967 receptor sequences x 58 columns; 770/772 receptor IDs in spatial data (99.7%) #> TCR: 0 receptor sequences x 58 columns; 0/0 receptor IDs in spatial data (NaN%) #> Spatial ID field: barcode_10x #> Analyses: 0 ``` `subsetSIRUP()` gives finer control. It can keep a set of spots or a set of receptor rows. With `keep_nonspatial_receptors = TRUE`, it also keeps the bulk rows. `mergeSIRUP()` goes the other way. It combines single-section objects into a multi-sample object, and it adds a sample column with the names that you give. ``` r slice2 <- filterSample(sirup, "mg_thymus_slice2") merged <- mergeSIRUP( slice1, slice2, samples = c("mg_thymus_slice1", "mg_thymus_slice2"), sample_field = "sample" ) merged #> #> Spatial data: Seurat, 6,599 spatial IDs, 449 genes, 2 spatial samples, 2 images #> Receptor data: 2 slots #> BCR: 4,072 receptor sequences x 58 columns; 1,567/1,640 receptor IDs in spatial data (95.5%) #> TCR: 3,610 receptor sequences x 58 columns; 1,414/1,571 receptor IDs in spatial data (90.0%) #> Samples: 2 #> Spatial ID field: barcode_10x #> Sample ID field: sample #> Analyses: 0 ``` ## Add polygons for each section A polygon is a closed outline that selects the spots of one tissue region. Give `addPolygons()` a named vector of polygon files, one for each section. ``` r sirup <- addPolygons(sirup, polygons_path = c( mg_thymus_slice1 = file.path(extdata, "mg_thymus_slice1_gc_polygons.csv"), mg_thymus_slice2 = file.path(extdata, "mg_thymus_slice2_gc_polygons.csv") )) getPolygons(sirup) #> # A tibble: 19 × 3 #> polygon_id sample vertices #> #> 1 mg_thymus_slice1::1 mg_thymus_slice1 #> 2 mg_thymus_slice1::10 mg_thymus_slice1 #> 3 mg_thymus_slice1::2 mg_thymus_slice1 #> 4 mg_thymus_slice1::3 mg_thymus_slice1 #> 5 mg_thymus_slice1::4 mg_thymus_slice1 #> 6 mg_thymus_slice1::5 mg_thymus_slice1 #> 7 mg_thymus_slice1::6 mg_thymus_slice1 #> 8 mg_thymus_slice1::7 mg_thymus_slice1 #> 9 mg_thymus_slice1::8 mg_thymus_slice1 #> 10 mg_thymus_slice1::9 mg_thymus_slice1 #> 11 mg_thymus_slice2::1 mg_thymus_slice2 #> 12 mg_thymus_slice2::2 mg_thymus_slice2 #> 13 mg_thymus_slice2::3 mg_thymus_slice2 #> 14 mg_thymus_slice2::4 mg_thymus_slice2 #> 15 mg_thymus_slice2::5 mg_thymus_slice2 #> 16 mg_thymus_slice2::6 mg_thymus_slice2 #> 17 mg_thymus_slice2::7 mg_thymus_slice2 #> 18 mg_thymus_slice2::8 mg_thymus_slice2 #> 19 mg_thymus_slice2::9 mg_thymus_slice2 ``` Both files number their eGCs from 1. SIRUP adds the sample to each polygon ID. `mg_thymus_slice1::1` and `mg_thymus_slice2::1` are different regions. ## Plot several sections A spatial plot of a multi-sample object returns a list with one plot for each section. Set `combine_sample_plots = TRUE` to get one combined figure. Give `sample_id` to plot one section. ``` r plotSpatialPolygons(sirup, zoom = TRUE, combine_sample_plots = TRUE) ``` ![](multisample_files/figure-gfm/plots-1.jpeg) ``` r spatialExpressionPlot( sirup, features = "AICDA", assay = "alra", layer = "data", sample_id = "mg_thymus_slice1", title = "AICDA, section 1" ) ``` ![](multisample_files/figure-gfm/plot-one-1.jpeg) ## Call clones across all samples Call clones on the whole BCR table. One clone ID then covers the sections, the bulk thymus, and the blood. ``` r sirup <- updateReceptors( sirup, scoper::hierarchicalClones, slot = "BCR", threshold = 0.1, summarize_clones = FALSE, nproc = 1 ) dplyr::n_distinct(getReceptors(sirup, slot = "BCR")$clone_id) #> [1] 1860 ``` ## Find where each clone was seen Each row has a `compartment`. For each clone, the code below counts the sequences in each compartment. It also records the eGCs that hold the clone. ``` r clones <- getReceptors(sirup, slot = "BCR") %>% group_by(clone_id) %>% summarise( in_section = any(compartment %in% c("thymus_slice1", "thymus_slice2")), n_egc = sum(!is.na(polygon_id)), egcs = paste(sort(unique(na.omit(polygon_id))), collapse = ", "), n_bulk_thymus = sum(compartment == "bulk_thymus"), n_blood_month0 = sum(compartment == "blood_month0"), n_blood_month12 = sum(compartment == "blood_month12") ) %>% mutate( in_egc = n_egc > 0, in_blood = n_blood_month0 + n_blood_month12 > 0 ) count(clones, in_egc, in_blood) #> # A tibble: 4 × 3 #> in_egc in_blood n #> #> 1 FALSE FALSE 1575 #> 2 FALSE TRUE 153 #> 3 TRUE FALSE 121 #> 4 TRUE TRUE 11 ``` The table shows that most clones stay in the thymus. A few eGC clones also appear in the blood. The SIRUP paper calls these clones exported. Fisher’s exact test compares the eGC clones with the other clones of the sections. ``` r section_clones <- filter(clones, in_section) fisher.test(table(section_clones$in_egc, section_clones$in_blood)) #> #> Fisher's Exact Test for Count Data #> #> data: table(section_clones$in_egc, section_clones$in_blood) #> p-value = 0.3623 #> alternative hypothesis: true odds ratio is not equal to 1 #> 95 percent confidence interval: #> 0.625789 2.559146 #> sample estimates: #> odds ratio #> 1.326868 ``` For each eGC, count the clones that it holds and the clones that reach the blood. ``` r getReceptors(sirup, slot = "BCR") %>% filter(!is.na(polygon_id)) %>% distinct(polygon_id, clone_id) %>% left_join(select(clones, clone_id, in_blood), by = "clone_id") %>% group_by(polygon_id) %>% summarise(n_clones = n(), n_exported = sum(in_blood)) %>% arrange(desc(n_exported)) #> # A tibble: 17 × 3 #> polygon_id n_clones n_exported #> #> 1 mg_thymus_slice2::5 23 5 #> 2 mg_thymus_slice2::1 16 3 #> 3 mg_thymus_slice1::10 15 1 #> 4 mg_thymus_slice1::2 2 1 #> 5 mg_thymus_slice2::2 16 1 #> 6 mg_thymus_slice2::3 7 1 #> 7 mg_thymus_slice2::6 4 1 #> 8 mg_thymus_slice1::1 6 0 #> 9 mg_thymus_slice1::3 2 0 #> 10 mg_thymus_slice1::4 1 0 #> 11 mg_thymus_slice1::5 10 0 #> 12 mg_thymus_slice1::6 18 0 #> 13 mg_thymus_slice1::7 2 0 #> 14 mg_thymus_slice1::9 5 0 #> 15 mg_thymus_slice2::7 12 0 #> 16 mg_thymus_slice2::8 4 0 #> 17 mg_thymus_slice2::9 4 0 ``` The bulk files hold a subset of the bulk data, and the clones come from that subset. For the full analysis, see Figure 5 of the SIRUP paper. ## Measure clonal dominance in each section Clonal dominance is the share of the receptors in a region that belong to its largest clones. The regional functions work on all sections at once. The dominance table has a `sample` column and the full `polygon_id`. For a longer treatment, see [Draw tissue regions and measure clonal dominance and diversity](regions.md). ``` r dominance <- spatialCloneDominance(object = sirup, slot = "BCR", locus_val = "IGH") dominance$dominance %>% group_by(polygon_id) %>% slice_max(proportion, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) %>% ungroup() %>% select(sample, polygon_id, clone_id, n_receptors, proportion) %>% head() #> # A tibble: 6 × 5 #> sample polygon_id clone_id n_receptors proportion #> #> 1 mg_thymus_slice1 mg_thymus_slice1::1 1270 2 0.222 #> 2 mg_thymus_slice1 mg_thymus_slice1::10 1148 4 0.16 #> 3 mg_thymus_slice1 mg_thymus_slice1::2 1661 1 0.5 #> 4 mg_thymus_slice1 mg_thymus_slice1::3 1267 2 0.5 #> 5 mg_thymus_slice1 mg_thymus_slice1::4 1399 1 1 #> 6 mg_thymus_slice1 mg_thymus_slice1::5 1385 3 0.231 ``` Most plotting functions return a named list with one plot for each section. ``` r region_plots <- plotSpatialRegionReceptors( dominance = dominance, object = sirup, top_n = 8, point_size = 1.5, zoom = TRUE ) names(region_plots) #> [1] "mg_thymus_slice1" "mg_thymus_slice2" region_plots$mg_thymus_slice1 ``` ![](multisample_files/figure-gfm/region-receptors-1.jpeg) `plotSpatialPolygonPies()` also works on all sections at once. Give `sample_id` to draw the pies of one section next to its map. ``` r pies <- plotSpatialPolygonPies( dominance = dominance, object = sirup, fill = "clone_id", top_n = 5, sample_id = "mg_thymus_slice1" ) pies$page_1 #> Warning: Removed 10 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range #> (`geom_text()`). ``` ![](multisample_files/figure-gfm/pies-1.jpeg) ## Build a tree with blood tips A lineage tree shows how the sequences of one clone relate to each other. Each tip of the tree is one sequence. A tree can mix spatial and bulk sequences. The code below picks an exported eGC clone with blood sequences from both time points. ``` r exported <- clones %>% filter(in_egc, n_blood_month0 > 0, n_blood_month12 > 0) %>% mutate(n_total = n_egc + n_bulk_thymus + n_blood_month0 + n_blood_month12) %>% filter(n_total <= 100) %>% arrange(desc(n_blood_month0 + n_blood_month12)) exported #> # A tibble: 4 × 10 #> clone_id in_section n_egc egcs n_bulk_thymus n_blood_month0 n_blood_month12 #> #> 1 1045 TRUE 2 mg_thy… 10 15 4 #> 2 1673 TRUE 3 mg_thy… 0 2 1 #> 3 868 TRUE 1 mg_thy… 0 1 2 #> 4 85 TRUE 1 mg_thy… 10 1 1 #> # ℹ 3 more variables: in_egc , in_blood , n_total tree_clone <- exported$clone_id[[1]] tree_section <- sub("::.*$", "", exported$egcs[[1]]) tree_section #> [1] "mg_thymus_slice2" ``` Make the germline of the clone with `dowser::createGermlines()`. The germline is the sequence of the unmutated ancestor, and the tree starts there. Then build the tree. As in [Call clones and build lineage trees on the tissue](clones-and-trees.md), the germline step needs the IMGT reference sequences. Set the environment variable `SIRUP_IMGT_DIR` to the folder that holds them. The tree chunks run only when that folder exists. Keep `compartment` in `traits`. The tree plot uses it to set the tip shapes. ``` r tree_sirup <- updateReceptors(sirup, dplyr::filter, clone_id == tree_clone, slot = "BCR") tree_sirup <- updateReceptors( tree_sirup, dowser::createGermlines, slot = "BCR", references = dowser::readIMGT(imgt_dir), id = "sequence_id" ) #> Warning in fun(sirup_data, ...): 107 sequence lengths longer than predicted #> germlines, consider setting trim_lengths=TRUE if germlines fail #> [1] "Read in 1198 from 17 fasta files" tree_sirup <- formatSpatialClones( tree_sirup, slot = "BCR", id = "sequence_id", traits = c("barcode_10x", "sample", "compartment", "polygon_id") ) set.seed(1) tree_sirup <- getSpatialTrees(tree_sirup, slot = "BCR") trees <- getAnalysis(tree_sirup, "trees_BCR") ``` `plotSpatialCloneTreePairs()` puts the spatial tips on their sections. Bulk and blood tips appear in the tree only. The argument `shape_by` sets one shape for each compartment. The argument `color_by` colors the tips by tree cluster. `clusterTreesTips()` makes the clusters. ``` r trees <- clusterTreesTips(trees, k = "auto", id = "sequence_id", k_range = 1:6) pair <- plotSpatialCloneTreePairs( trees, object = sirup, slot = "BCR", id = "sequence_id", color_by = "tree_cluster", shape_by = "compartment", shape_values = c( thymus_slice1 = 21, thymus_slice2 = 21, bulk_thymus = 22, blood_month0 = 24, blood_month12 = 23 ), zoom = TRUE, polygons = TRUE, polygon_alpha = 0, polygon_color = "black", show_spatial_legend = TRUE ) names(pair) #> [1] "1045" ``` The list has one element for each clone. If the tips of a clone fall in more than one section, the list has one element for each clone and section instead. These elements are named `::`. Each one pairs the full tree with the map of one section. Each element also holds a `legend` for the tip colors. The function builds it because the call sets `show_spatial_legend = TRUE`. The code below shows the section that holds the eGC tips. ``` r key <- paste0(tree_clone, "::", tree_section) if (!key %in% names(pair)) key <- tree_clone section_pair <- pair[[key]] cowplot::plot_grid( cowplot::plot_grid(section_pair$tree, section_pair$spatial_clone, rel_widths = c(1.3, 1)), section_pair$legend, ncol = 1, rel_heights = c(1, section_pair$legend_rel_height) ) ``` ![](multisample_files/figure-gfm/tree-plot-show-1.jpeg) Shapes show the compartment of each tip. Circles are tips from a section. Squares are bulk thymus. Triangles are blood at the thymectomy. Diamonds are blood 12 months later. The legend shows the colors, which are the tree clusters from `clusterTreesTips()`. On the map, a dot has the color of its tip. ## Save the object `saveSIRUP()` writes the whole object to one file. `readSIRUP()` reads it back and checks it. ``` r path <- file.path(tempdir(), "mg_thymus.sirup.rds") saveSIRUP(sirup, path) readSIRUP(path) #> #> Spatial data: Seurat, 6,599 spatial IDs, 449 genes, 2 spatial samples, 2 images #> Receptor data: 2 slots #> BCR: 5,537 receptor sequences x 79 columns; 1,567/1,640 receptor IDs in spatial data (95.5%) #> TCR: 3,610 receptor sequences x 68 columns; 1,414/1,571 receptor IDs in spatial data (90.0%) #> Samples: 2 #> Spatial ID field: barcode_10x #> Sample ID field: sample #> Clone ID field: clone_id #> Analyses: 0 #> Polygons: 19 ``` ## Next steps - Call clones and build trees for one section: [Call clones and build lineage trees on the tissue](clones-and-trees.md). - Draw tissue regions and measure clonal dominance and diversity: [Draw tissue regions and measure clonal dominance and diversity](regions.md). - Learn how SIRUP stores samples, polygons, and analyses: [How the SIRUP object works](sirup-object.md).

pages.title: How the SIRUP object works
pages.summary: Learn the five parts of a SIRUP object, the rules that SIRUP checks, and the functions that change the object.
pages.markdown:
How the SIRUP object works ================ A spatial receptor experiment gives you three kinds of data: gene expression for each spot, receptor sequences, and the regions that you draw on the tissue. These data must agree with each other. A receptor must belong to a spot that exists. A clone column must exist in the receptor table. The SIRUP object keeps all of the data in one place and checks these rules each time you change it. This page explains the parts of the object, the rules that SIRUP checks, and the functions that change the object. It has little code. For a hands-on start, read [Get started with SIRUP](get-started.md). The examples use a small synthetic object. It has 25 spots, 10 genes, 5 clones, and 2 polygons. The spots and gene counts are simulated. The receptor rows are real BCR sequences from a human thymus section, assigned to synthetic spots. ``` r library(SIRUP) x <- readSIRUP(system.file("extdata", "sirup_synthetic.rds", package = "SIRUP")) x #> #> Spatial data: Seurat, 25 spatial IDs, 10 genes, 0 images #> Receptor data: tibble, 36 receptor sequences x 64 columns #> Spatial overlap: 19/19 receptor IDs in spatial data (100.0%) #> Spatial ID field: spatial_id #> Clone ID field: clone_id #> Analyses: 0 #> Polygons: 2 ``` ## The five parts A SIRUP object is a list with five parts, in this order: | Part | Contents | How to get it | |----|----|----| | `spatial` | The Seurat object, with expression and the H&E image | `getSpatial(x)` | | `receptors` | The AIRR receptor table, as a tibble, or a named list of tables | `getReceptors(x)` | | `metadata` | The field names and the image settings | `x$metadata` | | `polygons` | The tissue regions, with one row for each polygon | `getPolygons(x)` | | `analyses` | Results that you choose to keep | `getAnalysis(x, name)` | The accessors return ordinary R objects. You can pass them to any function from another package: ``` r getSpatial(x) #> An object of class Seurat #> 10 features across 25 samples within 1 assay #> Active assay: Spatial (10 features, 0 variable features) #> 1 layer present: counts head(getReceptors(x), 3) #> # A tibble: 3 × 64 #> sequence_id spatial_id clone_id locus sequence rev_comp productive v_call #> #> 1 seq01 spot21 1 IGH CAGGTGCATCTG… FALSE TRUE IGHV1… #> 2 seq02 spot19 1 IGH CAGGTGCATCTG… FALSE TRUE IGHV1… #> 3 seq03 spot16 1 IGH CAGGTGCATCTG… FALSE TRUE IGHV1… #> # ℹ 56 more variables: d_call , j_call , sequence_alignment , #> # germline_alignment , junction , junction_aa , v_cigar , #> # d_cigar , j_cigar , stop_codon , vj_in_frame , #> # c_call , junction_length , np1_length , np2_length , #> # v_sequence_start , v_sequence_end , v_germline_start , #> # v_germline_end , d_sequence_start , d_sequence_end , #> # d_germline_start , d_germline_end , j_sequence_start , … getPolygons(x) #> # A tibble: 2 × 2 #> polygon_id vertices #> #> 1 upper_right #> 2 lower_left ``` `summary()` gives counts for each part: ``` r summary(x) #> SIRUP summary #> Spatial IDs: 25 #> Receptor records: 36 #> Receptor IDs: 19 #> Matched IDs: 19 (100.0%) #> Matched records: 36 #> Image scale: hires #> Swap coords: FALSE #> Stored analyses: 0 #> Polygons: 2 #> #> Per-sample summary #> # A tibble: 1 × 7 #> sample n_spatial_ids n_receptor_records n_receptor_ids n_matched_ids #> #> 1 spatial 25 36 19 19 #> # ℹ 2 more variables: n_matched_records , id_match_rate ``` ## Field names Your receptor table can use any column names. SIRUP needs to know which column plays which role. It stores this map in `x$metadata$receptor_fields`. There are six fields: | Field | The receptor column that holds… | |----|----| | `spatial_id` | the name of the spot that holds the receptor | | `image` | the name of the Seurat image, if the object has several images | | `sample` | the sample name, in a multi-sample object | | `clone` | the clone ID | | `locus` | the receptor locus, such as `IGH` or `TRB` | | `count` | the number of reads or UMIs of the sequence | ``` r x$metadata$receptor_fields #> $spatial_id #> [1] "spatial_id" #> #> $image #> NULL #> #> $sample #> NULL #> #> $clone #> [1] "clone_id" #> #> $locus #> [1] "locus" #> #> $count #> NULL ``` You set the fields once, in `createSIRUP()`. After that, SIRUP functions find each column without arguments. To change a field later, give a new map to `updateReceptors()` with the `receptor_fields` argument. A value of `NULL` clears an optional field. ## Rules that SIRUP checks `validateSIRUP()` checks that the parts agree. It gives an error if one of these rules fails: 1. The object has class `sirup`. 2. At least one receptor spatial ID matches a spot name in the Seurat object. 3. Each column that `receptor_fields` names exists in the receptor table. If the object has several receptor tables, the spatial ID column must be in every table. Each other named column, such as `clone_id`, must be in at least one table. 4. If the `sample` field is set, the column exists in every receptor table and in the Seurat metadata. ``` r validateSIRUP(x, verbose = TRUE) #> #> Spatial data: Seurat, 25 spatial IDs, 10 genes, 0 images #> Receptor data: tibble, 36 receptor sequences x 64 columns #> Spatial overlap: 19/19 receptor IDs in spatial data (100.0%) #> Spatial ID field: spatial_id #> Clone ID field: clone_id #> Analyses: 0 #> Polygons: 2 ``` `createSIRUP()`, `updateReceptors()`, `updateSpatial()`, and the other functions that change the object run this check before they return. A change that breaks a rule fails at once and leaves your object as it was. This example gives every receptor a spot name that does not exist: ``` r tryCatch( updateReceptors(x, function(receptors) { receptors$spatial_id <- "no-such-spot" receptors }), error = function(e) conditionMessage(e) ) #> [1] "No receptor IDs match the spatial Seurat object." ```

Note

SIRUP keeps receptor rows that match no spot. Bulk and blood sequences are examples. The rules need only one match, so these rows stay in the table.
## Image settings Two settings tell SIRUP how to put spots on the H&E image. Both live in `x$metadata`: - `image_scale` is the Seurat image scale, `"lowres"` or `"hires"`. - `swap_coords` says whether to swap the x and y coordinates. Some older Seurat objects store the coordinates in the opposite order to the image. Plots and spatial statistics read these settings when you leave their own `image_scale` and `swap_coords` arguments at `NULL`. You set them once. ## Change the data SIRUP does not wrap every AIRR tool. Three functions run any function on one part of the object and put the result back: - `updateReceptors(x, fun, ...)` calls `fun(getReceptors(x), ...)` and stores the table that `fun` returns. - `updateSpatial(x, fun, ...)` calls `fun(getSpatial(x), ...)` and stores the Seurat object that `fun` returns. - `updateAnalysis(x, name, fun, ...)` does the same for a stored analysis. Each function validates the object again before it returns. This call removes the sequences of one clone: ``` r x2 <- updateReceptors(x, dplyr::filter, clone_id != "3") c(before = nrow(getReceptors(x)), after = nrow(getReceptors(x2))) #> before after #> 36 29 ``` This call adds a column to the Seurat metadata: ``` r x3 <- updateSpatial(x, function(spatial) { spatial$gene_rich <- spatial$nFeature_Spatial >= 8 spatial }) table(getSpatial(x3)$gene_rich) #> #> FALSE TRUE #> 2 23 ``` The same pattern runs germline reconstruction (`dowser::createGermlines()`) or mutation counting (`shazam::observedMutations()`) inside the object. [Call clones and build lineage trees on the tissue](clones-and-trees.md) shows these steps. ## Regions in the object A region is a polygon on the tissue image. `addPolygons()` stores the polygons and then marks the polygon of each spot and each receptor. It adds a `polygon_id` column and one logical `polygon_` column for each polygon to both the Seurat metadata and the receptor table: ``` r grep("^polygon", names(getReceptors(x)), value = TRUE) #> [1] "polygon_id" "polygon_upper_right" "polygon_lower_left" grep("^polygon", names(getSpatial(x)[[]]), value = TRUE) #> [1] "polygon_id" "polygon_upper_right" "polygon_lower_left" ``` A spot on the edge of a polygon counts as a member when `include_boundary` is `TRUE`, which is the default. [Draw tissue regions and measure clonal dominance and diversity](regions.md) shows how to draw regions and measure what they hold. ## Several samples `createSIRUP()` accepts one Seurat object or a named list of Seurat objects. With a list, the `sample` column of the receptor table names the list entry of each row. Rows with no matching entry stay in the table as non-spatial records. Bulk and blood sequences use this feature. `mergeSIRUP()` joins several objects into one. `subsetSIRUP()` keeps chosen samples, spots, or receptor rows. `getSpatial()` and `getReceptors()` return the data of one sample when you give `sample_id`. [Analyze several sections with bulk AIRR-seq and blood](multisample.md) has a full example. ## Several receptor tables One object can hold more than one receptor table, for example one table of BCRs and one of TCRs. Give `createSIRUP()` a named list of tables. Each table is a *slot*. All slots share the spatial data, the polygons, and the field names. The spatial ID column must be in every table. A column such as `clone_id` can be in one table only, for example in the BCR table. Clone IDs only need to be unique within one slot. ``` r bcr <- getReceptors(x) tcr <- bcr[1:8, ] tcr$locus <- "TRB" both <- createSIRUP( spatial = getSpatial(x), receptors = list(bcr = bcr, tcr = tcr), spatial_id = "spatial_id", clone = "clone_id", image_scale = "hires", swap_coords = FALSE, polygons = getPolygons(x) ) receptorSlots(both) #> [1] "bcr" "tcr" both #> #> Spatial data: Seurat, 25 spatial IDs, 10 genes, 0 images #> Receptor data: 2 slots #> bcr: 36 receptor sequences x 64 columns; 19/19 receptor IDs in spatial data (100.0%) #> tcr: 8 receptor sequences x 64 columns; 8/8 receptor IDs in spatial data (100.0%) #> Spatial ID field: spatial_id #> Clone ID field: clone_id #> Analyses: 0 #> Polygons: 2 ``` Functions that use receptors work on one slot at a time. Choose the slot with the `slot` argument. If the object has several slots, you must give `slot`. If the object has one table, leave it out. That table has the slot name `"only_slot"`. ``` r head(getReceptors(both, slot = "tcr"), 3) #> # A tibble: 3 × 64 #> sequence_id spatial_id clone_id locus sequence rev_comp productive v_call #> #> 1 seq01 spot21 1 TRB CAGGTGCATCTG… FALSE TRUE IGHV1… #> 2 seq02 spot19 1 TRB CAGGTGCATCTG… FALSE TRUE IGHV1… #> 3 seq03 spot16 1 TRB CAGGTGCATCTG… FALSE TRUE IGHV1… #> # ℹ 56 more variables: d_call , j_call , sequence_alignment , #> # germline_alignment , junction , junction_aa , v_cigar , #> # d_cigar , j_cigar , stop_codon , vj_in_frame , #> # c_call , junction_length , np1_length , np2_length , #> # v_sequence_start , v_sequence_end , v_germline_start , #> # v_germline_end , d_sequence_start , d_sequence_end , #> # d_germline_start , d_germline_end , j_sequence_start , … both <- polygonReceptorSummary(both, slot = "tcr") listAnalyses(both) #> [1] "polygon_receptor_summary_tcr" tryCatch(getReceptors(both), error = function(e) conditionMessage(e)) #> [1] "`slot` is required because this SIRUP object has several receptor slots.\nℹ Slots: bcr, tcr." ``` The polygons apply to every slot. A receptor is in a polygon if it is in the same sample and its spatial ID lies inside the polygon. The default analysis names end with the slot name, so results for different slots do not overwrite each other. ## Keep results with the data `setAnalysis()` stores any R object under a name. Use it for clones, trees, spatial statistics, and polygon summaries. Stored results stay with the data that made them, so you do not track separate files: ``` r x <- setAnalysis(x, "n_clones", 5) listAnalyses(x) #> [1] "n_clones" getAnalysis(x, "n_clones") #> [1] 5 x <- removeAnalysis(x, "n_clones") listAnalyses(x) #> character(0) ``` `saveSIRUP()` validates the object and writes it to one RDS file. The file also records the versions of SIRUP and SeuratObject that wrote it. `readSIRUP()` reads the file and does four things. It converts an object saved under the old package name (SIRAP). It upgrades an older object to the current layout. It warns you if the package versions differ from the file. It validates the object. ``` r path <- saveSIRUP(x, tempfile(fileext = ".sirup.rds")) x_again <- readSIRUP(path) x_again #> #> Spatial data: Seurat, 25 spatial IDs, 10 genes, 0 images #> Receptor data: tibble, 36 receptor sequences x 64 columns #> Spatial overlap: 19/19 receptor IDs in spatial data (100.0%) #> Spatial ID field: spatial_id #> Clone ID field: clone_id #> Analyses: 0 #> Polygons: 2 ``` ## Next steps - To build an object from your own data, follow [Get started with SIRUP](get-started.md). - To work with regions, read [Draw tissue regions and measure clonal dominance and diversity](regions.md). - To combine sections, bulk data, and blood, read [Analyze several sections with bulk AIRR-seq and blood](multisample.md).

pages.title: Choose a spatial statistic
pages.summary: Pick a spatial statistic by the question you ask: clustering, co-variation, nearness of two spot types, or the spread of a clone.
pages.markdown:
Choose a spatial statistic
================

This guide helps you choose an appropriate spatial statistic to answer
the question you want to ask. Each section below names one question. It
then gives the function, the input, and how to understand the results.

A few definitions: A *spot* is spatially-resolved location where we
capture gene expression or a BCR/TCR sequence. A *clone* is a group of
cells that are inferred to descend from a common ancestor. *Spatial
autocorrelation* is the tendency of nearby spots to have similar values,
i.e., high values by high values and low values by low values.

All tests need a SIRUP object, or a Seurat object with spatial images.
The tests read the spot coordinates from the object. Most tests compare
each spot with its “neighbors”. Generally, you can set the number of
neighbors with `k` (i.e., the `k` nearest spots will be neighbors) or
`radius` (which draws a circle with radius `radius` around the point in
question and all points inside that circle are neighbors of the point).

## Match the question to the function

| Question | Function | Input |
|----|----|----|
| Is a continuous variable spatially autocorrelated? | `spatialMoran()` | One gene or numeric metadata column |
| Where is a continuous variable spatially autocorrelated? | `spatialLocalMoran()` | One gene or numeric metadata column |
| Do two continuous variables co-vary in space? | `spatialLee()` | Two continuous variables |
| How far does a clone spread? | `spatialCloneSpread()` | Receptor table with clone IDs, pass the ID of the clone you’re interested in |
| Is a discrete variable (in this case a particular clone) spatially autocorrelated? | `spatialCloneJoinCount()` | Receptor table with clone IDs, pass the ID of the clone you’re interested in |
| Do two discrete variables co-vary in space? | `spatialRipleyCrossK()` | One metadata column with two labels |

## Set up the example data

The examples use one myasthenia gravis (MG) thymus section. This code
downloads the example files, which are not part of the SIRUP package.
Change `dest` to a folder you want to keep. The function skips files
that are already there.

``` r
extdata <- SIRUP::downloadSIRUPExample(
  dest = file.path(tempdir(), "SIRUP_example"),
  files = c(
    "mg_thymus_cell_types.csv.gz",
    "mg_thymus_slice2_bcr.tsv.gz",
    "mg_thymus_slice2_tcr.tsv.gz",
    "mg_thymus_slice2_gc_polygons.csv",
    "mg_thymus_slice2_spatial.rds"
  )
)
#> ℹ Downloading 'mg_thymus_cell_types.csv.gz'
#> ℹ Downloading 'mg_thymus_slice2_bcr.tsv.gz'
#> ℹ Downloading 'mg_thymus_slice2_tcr.tsv.gz'
#> ℹ Downloading 'mg_thymus_slice2_gc_polygons.csv'
#> ℹ Downloading 'mg_thymus_slice2_spatial.rds'
```

Then build a SIRUP object from the spatial data, the cell-type
estimates, and the BCRs and TCRs. Then call the BCR clones.
[Test spatial patterns of genes, cells, and clones](spatial-statistics.md) explains each step.

``` r
library(SIRUP)
library(dplyr)

thymus <- readRDS(file.path(extdata, "mg_thymus_slice2_spatial.rds"))

cell_types <- data.table::fread(
  file.path(extdata, "mg_thymus_cell_types.csv.gz"),
  data.table = FALSE
) %>%
  filter(sample == "mg_thymus_slice2")
rownames(cell_types) <- cell_types$barcode
thymus <- Seurat::AddMetaData(thymus, select(cell_types, -sample, -barcode))

bcrs <- airr::read_rearrangement(file.path(extdata, "mg_thymus_slice2_bcr.tsv.gz")) %>%
  extractSpatialIds(
    id = "sequence_id",
    spatial_id = "barcode_10x",
    regex = ",([ACGT]{16})$",
    suffix = "-1"
  ) %>%
  filterAirr(
    locus_val = "IGH",
    min_v_length = 250,
    min_j_length = 30,
    min_junction_length = 10,
    productive_only = TRUE,
    min_consensus_count = NULL,
    spatial_id = "barcode_10x"
  ) %>%
  filter(!grepl("[^ACGT]", junction))
tcrs <- airr::read_rearrangement(file.path(extdata, "mg_thymus_slice2_tcr.tsv.gz")) %>%
  extractSpatialIds(
    id = "sequence_id",
    spatial_id = "barcode_10x",
    regex = ",([ACGT]{16})$",
    suffix = "-1"
  ) %>%
  filterAirr(
    locus_val = "TRB",
    min_v_length = 250,
    min_j_length = 30,
    min_junction_length = 10,
    productive_only = TRUE,
    min_consensus_count = NULL,
    spatial_id = "barcode_10x"
  ) %>%
  filter(!grepl("[^ACGT]", junction))

x <- createSIRUP(
  spatial = thymus,
  receptors = list(BCR = bcrs, TCR = tcrs),
  spatial_id = "barcode_10x",
  image_scale = "lowres",
  swap_coords = FALSE,
  polygons_path = file.path(extdata, "mg_thymus_slice2_gc_polygons.csv")
)
x <- updateReceptors(
  x,
  scoper::hierarchicalClones,
  slot = "BCR",
  threshold = 0.1,
  summarize_clones = FALSE,
  nproc = 1
)
```

## Is a continuous variable spatially autocorrelated?

Use `spatialMoran()` to determine if a continuous variable is spatially
autocorrelated, i.e., if neighboring spots have similar values. This
function computes [Moran’s
I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moran%27s_I#Global_Moran's_I). Moran’s
I is near 0 when the values show no spatial pattern, it is positive when
similar values are nearby, and it is negative when dissimilar values are
nearby.

The input is a SIRUP or Seurat object. `variable_type` tells the
function what type of variable it is: a gene (`"feature"`) or a numeric
metadata column (`"metadata"`). `k` is the number of neighbors.

The estimate $I$ and the associated p value are reported. Note that a
larger section can inflate significance, so you may see a tiny p value
for a weak pattern in larger datasets.

See the code below for an example on the thymus section.

``` r
moran <- spatialMoran(
  x,
  variable = "GC B",
  variable_type = "metadata",
  k = 6
)
moran$test$estimate[[1]]
#> [1] 0.6229165
moran$test$p.value
#> [1] 0
```

## **Where** is a continuous variable spatially autocorrelated?

Use `spatialLocalMoran()` to find where a continuous variable is
spatially autocorrelated, i.e., which spots sit in a cluster of similar
values. This function computes [local Moran’s
I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moran%27s_I#Local_Moran's_I) (also
called LISA) for each spot. Local Moran’s I is positive when a spot has
neighbors with similar values and negative when a spot differs from its
neighbors.

The input is a SIRUP or Seurat object. `variable_type` tells the
function what type of variable it is: a gene (`"feature"`) or a numeric
metadata column (`"metadata"`). `k` is the number of neighbors.

The result has one row for each spot, with the local I (`local_i`), a
z-score (`z_i`), and a p value (`p_value`). Each spot has its own p
value, so we should adjust for multiple testing.
`plotSpatialLocalMoran()` draws the z-scores on the tissue.

See the code below for an example on the thymus section.

``` r
local_moran <- spatialLocalMoran(
  x,
  variable = "GC B",
  variable_type = "metadata",
  k = 6
)
head(local_moran[, c("cell", "local_i", "z_i", "p_value")])
#>                 cell    local_i       z_i     p_value
#> 1 AAACAAGTATCTCCCA-1 0.42119564 1.8775350 0.060444809
#> 2 AAACACCAATAACTGC-1 0.02554433 0.1780355 0.858695126
#> 3 AAACAGCTTTCAGAAG-1 0.67548360 2.1434191 0.032079462
#> 4 AAACAGGGTCTATATT-1 0.44557822 1.5436247 0.122679267
#> 5 AAACAGTGTTCCTGGG-1 0.10316582 0.6444111 0.519308914
#> 6 AAACATGGTGAGAGGA-1 2.05891309 3.0435870 0.002337758
plotSpatialLocalMoran(x, local_moran, point_size = 1)
```

![](choose-spatial-statistic_files/figure-gfm/local-moran-1.jpeg)

## Do two continuous variables co-vary in space?

Use `spatialLee()` to determine if two continuous variables share a
spatial pattern, i.e., if a high value of one variable tends to sit near
high values of the other. This function computes [Lee’s
L](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lee%27s_L). Lee’s L is near 0 when the
variables show no shared pattern, it is positive when both variables are
high (or both low) in the same neighborhoods, and it is negative when
one variable is high where the other is low.

The input is a SIRUP object or a Seurat object. `x` and `y` are the
names of the two variables, and `x_type` and `y_type` tell the function
what type each variable is: a gene (`"feature"`) or a numeric metadata
column (`"metadata"`). `k` is the number of neighbors.

The estimate $L$ and the associated p value are reported. The default
test (`method = "analytical"`) builds a dense matrix with one entry for
each pair of spots, so it needs a lot of memory for large datasets. For
large data, such as Visium HD, set `method = "mc"` to use a permutation
test.

See the code below for an example on the thymus section.

``` r
lee <- spatialLee(
  x,
  x = "AICDA", x_type = "feature",
  y = "MS4A1", y_type = "feature",
  assay = "Spatial", layer = "data",
  k = 6
)
lee$L
#> [1] 0.09748529
lee$test$p.value
#> [1] 2.174023e-49
```

## How far does a clone spread?

Use `spatialCloneSpread()` to determine how far clones spread across the
tissue, i.e., how far apart their or sequences are. This function is
just descriptive. For each clone, it computes the distance between every
pair of points and reports the mean and the maximum of those distances.

The input is a SIRUP object or receptor table with clone IDs and spatial
IDs. A clone needs at least `min_spatial_ids` points (default 2). By
default, each sequence is a point, so sequences in the same spot give
distances of 0. Set `collapse_within_spot = TRUE` to count each spot
once.

The result has one row for each sample and clone, with the number of
spots (`n_spatial_ids`), the mean distance (`mean_pairwise_distance`),
and the maximum distance (`max_pairwise_distance`). Distances are in
image pixels.

See the code below for an example on the thymus section.

``` r
spread <- spatialCloneSpread(x, slot = "BCR", min_spatial_ids = 3)
spread %>%
  arrange(desc(n_spatial_ids)) %>%
  head()
#> # A tibble: 6 × 5
#>   sample  clone_id n_spatial_ids mean_pairwise_distance max_pairwise_distance
#>   <chr>   <chr>            <int>                  <dbl>                 <dbl>
#> 1 spatial 34                  86                   66.2                 397. 
#> 2 spatial 288                 42                  123.                  304. 
#> 3 spatial 196                 38                  156.                  395. 
#> 4 spatial 739                 16                   21.5                  75.1
#> 5 spatial 810                 14                   80.0                 263. 
#> 6 spatial 907                 14                   54.2                 120.
```

## Is a discrete variable (i.e., a particular clone) spatially autocorrelated?

Use `spatialCloneJoinCount()` to determine if a discrete variable is
spatially autocorrelated. This function computes the [join count
statistic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Join_count_statistic). Here,
the variable is whether a spot holds a particular clone, i.e., if the
spots of a clone sit next to each other. This function marks the spots
that hold the clone, counts the neighbor pairs in which both spots hold
the clone (the joins), and compares that count with the count expected
by chance. The observed count is higher than expected when the sequences
in the clone stay nearby each other.

The input is a SIRUP object receptor table with clone IDs and spatial
IDs. By default, the function tests every clone that occurs in at least
`min_spatial_ids` spots. Give `clone_val` to test chosen clones. If the
object has stored polygons, the function runs one test for each polygon.
Set `use_stored_polygons = FALSE` to run one test over the entire
section in this case.

The `summary` table has one row for each clone, with the observed and
expected join counts, a z-score (`statistic`), and a p value
(`p_value`). The default alternative is `"greater"`, so the test looks
for more joins than chance. The function tests many clones at once, so
be sure to adjust for multiple testing.

See the code below for an example on the thymus section.

``` r
big_clones <- getReceptors(x, slot = "BCR") %>%
  filter(!is.na(barcode_10x)) %>%
  distinct(clone_id, barcode_10x) %>%
  count(clone_id, sort = TRUE) %>%
  slice_head(n = 5) %>%
  pull(clone_id)

join_count <- spatialCloneJoinCount(
  x,
  slot = "BCR",
  clone_val = big_clones,
  use_stored_polygons = FALSE,
  k = 6,
  return_data = TRUE
)
join_count$summary[, c("clone_id", "observed_join_count", "expected_join_count", "p_value")]
#>   clone_id observed_join_count expected_join_count      p_value
#> 1      598                12.5           0.4145729 1.855757e-89
#> 2      288                30.0           2.6457286 1.118248e-74
#> 3       34                67.5          16.1683417 1.117067e-47
#> 4       64                 5.5           0.3391960 1.842208e-21
#> 5      196                15.5           2.6457286 4.997114e-18

plotSpatialCloneJoinCount(
  join_count = join_count,
  object = x,
  clone_val = join_count$summary$clone_id[[1]],
  show_neighbors = TRUE
)
```

![](choose-spatial-statistic_files/figure-gfm/join-count-1.jpeg)

## Do two discrete variables co-vary in space?

Use `spatialRipleyCrossK()` to determine if two discrete variables
co-vary in space, i.e., if spots of type A lie near spots of type B.
This function computes [Ripley’s cross
K](https://academicweb.nd.edu/~mhaenggi/ee87021/Dixon-K-Function.pdf?utm_campaign=redirect&utm_medium=web&utm_source=www3.nd.edu).
It counts the spots of type B within each distance of an average spot of
type A. It then compares that curve with curves from random relabeling
of the spots, which gives an envelope. Ripley’s cross K is similar to
Lee’s L, but it works with discrete data rather than continuous.

The input is a SIRUP object or a Seurat object with a column that holds
the labels (`mark_col`). Give the two levels to compare as `i` and `j`.
Set `nsim` above 0 to generate the randomly relabeled envelope for
comparison. Spots with `NA` in the column are left out.

The result holds the observed K at each distance (`plot_data`). A curve
above the envelope means that A and B sit closer than chance, i.e., they
**colocalize**. A curve below the envelope means that A and B are.
`plotRipleyCrossK()` draws the curve and the envelope. The distance is
in image pixels at the stored `image_scale`.

See the code below for an example on the thymus section.

``` r
# Label spots with mostly GC B cells or mostly T follicular helper (Tfh) cells.
x <- updateSpatial(x, function(spatial) {
  gc_b <- spatial$`GC B` > 0.10
  tfh <- spatial$Tfh > 0.10
  spatial$gc_tfh_mark <- case_when(
    gc_b & !tfh ~ "GC B",
    tfh & !gc_b ~ "Tfh",
    TRUE ~ NA_character_
  )
  spatial
})

set.seed(1)
kcross <- spatialRipleyCrossK(
  x,
  mark_col = "gc_tfh_mark",
  i = "GC B",
  j = "Tfh",
  nsim = 39,
  max_r = 40
)
plotRipleyCrossK(kcross, title = "Cross K: GC B spots to Tfh spots")
```

![](choose-spatial-statistic_files/figure-gfm/ripley-1.jpeg)

## Next steps

- Run tests on real data:
  [Test spatial patterns of genes, cells, and clones](spatial-statistics.md).
- Draw regions and measure their repertoires:
  [Draw tissue regions and measure clonal dominance and diversity](regions.md).
- Call clones before you test them:
  [Call clones and build lineage trees on the tissue](clones-and-trees.md).

pages.title: Use SIRUP with your LLM agent
pages.summary: Give an LLM agent such as Claude Code, Codex, or Antigravity the SIRUP skill or the llms files, and work with it on spatial receptor data.
pages.markdown:
Use SIRUP with your LLM agent ================ An LLM agent can write and run SIRUP code for you, and it can write better code when it knows how SIRUP works. SIRUP provides agents with: \* a packaged skill \* the llms files, which are text and JSON copies of the documentation. ## How to teach your agent about SIRUP | Method | What is it? | When to choose this? | |----|----|----| | The SIRUP skill | An agent skill | Your agent supports skills. Claude Code, Codex, and Antigravity (and likely others) do. | | The llms files | Text and JSON copies of the documentation | Your agent does not support skills or you do not wish to use one. | | The readthedocs pages | The pages of this site | You don’t want to upload files to your agent, and it can browse the web. | ## Install the skill Agent Skills is an open format created by Anthropic, and it is descrbied at [agentskills.io](https://agentskills.io). A skill is a folder with a file named `SKILL.md` that explains how to accomplish a task in a certain way to an agent. The file starts with a name and a description. At the start of a session, the agent reads the name and the description of each installed skill. It reads the rest of the folder only when you request that it uses the skill. SIRUP ships its skill inside the R package, in `inst/skills/sirup`, which is automatically copied into the package folder when you install a package in R. This puts the skill in your R library, so we need to put it in a place that your agent will look. For convenience, the `installSIRUPSkill()` function copies the skill to the appropriate location for Claude, Codex, and Antigravity agents. ``` r library(SIRUP) installSIRUPSkill(agent = "claude") # Claude Code installSIRUPSkill(agent = "codex") # Codex installSIRUPSkill(agent = "antigravity") # Antigravity ``` Run the line for your agent. By default, the function installs the skill in the folder that the agent reads for all your projects. | `agent` | Skill folder for all projects | | |-------------------------------|-------------------------------|-----| | `"claude"` (Claude Code) | `~/.claude/skills/` | | | `"codex"` (Codex) | `~/.agents/skills/` | | | `"antigravity"` (Antigravity) | `~/.gemini/config/skills/` | | If you only wish to install a skill for a particular project, use the `install_dir` argument. Claude agents read `.claude/skills/` in the project, and Codex and Antigravity agents read `.agents/skills/` in the project. ``` r installSIRUPSkill(agent = "claude", install_dir = ".claude/skills") installSIRUPSkill(agent = "codex", install_dir = ".agents/skills") installSIRUPSkill(agent = "antigravity", install_dir = ".agents/skills") ```

WARNING

These skill locations are correct as of late 2026. Updated architectures or other agent platforms may change them.
You can also copy the skill by hand. `system.file("skills", "sirup", package = "SIRUP")` returns the path of the skill folder. Copy that folder into the skills folder of your agent. ### Check that your agent sees the skill Start a new session. Ask the agent which skills it has, and look for `sirup`. Alternatively use `/skills` in a command line interface to list all available skills. In the Antigravity editor, open the Customizations menu in the agent panel. If you add a skill while an agent runs, restart the agent or reload skills (as with `/reload-skills` for Claude) first to see the new skill. ### Update the skill New SIRUP versions automatically keep the skill updated. After you update SIRUP, run `installSIRUPSkill()` once again. It replaces the old copy by default. ## Use the llms files instead The SIRUP repository holds four files specfically for LLMs. | File | Content | |------------------|---------------------------------------------------------| | `llms.txt` | A short Markdown index of the documentation, with links | | `llms.json` | The same short index in JSON | | `llms-full.txt` | The whole set of documentation in one text file | | `llms-full.json` | The whole set of documentation in JSON | Give an agent that has no skill support the address of `llms.json` or `llms.txt`. Tell it to read the index and then to fetch the page that it needs. The full files are large, about 400 KB each, so chat windows may not be able to hold them. We recommend that you start with the short index. ## Example requests Use these requests with the skill installed. Replace the file names with your own. ``` I have a Seurat object in `spatial.rds` and a corresponding spatial AIRR rearrangement in `bcr.tsv.gz`. Please build a SIRUP object and then build clones. Tell me how many sequences you removed and why. Which spatial statistic should I use to test whether one clone stays in one place? Load the region polygons in polygons.csv. Which clones dominate each region? Build lineage trees for the three largest clones in region 5. Tell me what the run needs before you start. Write a Slurm script that runs `processSpatialSample()` on my demultiplexed reads. This error came from `createSIRUP()`: . Can you please explain it and fix the call? ``` ## Work with an agent with care - **Read the code before you run it.** Ask the agent to explain each step. - **Protect private data.** A hosted agent sends your requests, and the files that it reads, to its provider. Check your data agreement before you share patient data. The example data that comes with SIRUP is for tutorials. - **Ask for checks.** Ask the agent to print the receptor count before and after each change, and to run `validateSIRUP()`. - **Ask what the agent did not run.** An agent can describe a result that it did not produce. - **Agents cannot draw ROIs.** Unless you give your agent a skill that allows it to click, you will have to draw regions with the polygon selection RShiny app. These can be subjective at times, so we recommend not passing this task to an agent. **An agent does not replace an expert review of your results.**

functions.title: Add quality measures to an AIRR table
functions.summary: `addSequenceQualityMetrics` adds columns that can help indicate the quality of each consensus sequence.
functions.markdown:
# addSequenceQualityMetrics

## Add quality measures to an AIRR table

## Description

`addSequenceQualityMetrics` adds columns that can help indicate the quality of each consensus sequence. It keeps all rows.

## Usage

``` R
addSequenceQualityMetrics(
  airr_df,
  sequence = "sequence",
  alignment = "sequence_alignment"
)
```

## Arguments

`airr_df`

:   AIRR-style data frame.

`sequence`

:   Name of the sequence column for the share of called bases (default `"sequence"`).

`alignment`

:   Name of the alignment column for the gap measures (default `"sequence_alignment"`).

## Details

Use this function to look at the distributions of the measures before you choose the thresholds for [`filterAirr()`](filterAirr.md). [`collapseTopConsensusPerSpatialId()`](collapseTopConsensusPerSpatialId.md) also adds these columns, but it removes rows.

The function adds these columns, if the source column exists:

- `non_N_nucleotide_prop`: the share of called bases (`A`, `C`, `G`, `T`) in `sequence`. A low value means an ambiguous consensus. The function takes this value from the ungapped sequence. The alignment would put IMGT gap characters in the denominator.

- `max_gap_length`: the longest run of gap characters in `alignment`.

- `opening_gap_length`: the gap run at the start of `alignment`.

## Value

`airr_df` with the quality columns added.

## See Also

[`filterAirr()`](filterAirr.md), [`collapseTopConsensusPerSpatialId()`](collapseTopConsensusPerSpatialId.md)

## Examples

``` R
x <- readSIRUP(system.file("extdata", "sirup_synthetic.rds", package = "SIRUP"))
metrics <- addSequenceQualityMetrics(getReceptors(x))
head(metrics[, c("non_N_nucleotide_prop", "max_gap_length", "opening_gap_length")])
```
