functions.markdown:
# addTissuePositions

## Add tissue coordinates to an AIRR table

## Description

`addTissuePositions` joins the tissue positions of the spots to an AIRR table. It adds the columns `x` and `y`.

## Usage

``` R
addTissuePositions(
  airr_df,
  positions,
  spatial_id = "spatial_id_8um",
  position_spatial_id = "barcode",
  x = "pxl_col_in_fullres",
  y = "pxl_row_in_fullres",
  keep_position_cols = TRUE
)
```

## Arguments

`airr_df`

:   AIRR-style data frame with a spatial ID column.

`positions`

:   Data frame of tissue positions, or the path of a CSV or parquet file.

`spatial_id`

:   Name of the column in `airr_df` to match (default `"spatial_id_8um"`).

`position_spatial_id`

:   Name of the spatial ID column in `positions` (default `"barcode"`).

`x`

:   Name of the column in `positions` to copy to `x` (default `"pxl_col_in_fullres"`).

`y`

:   Name of the column in `positions` to copy to `y` (default `"pxl_row_in_fullres"`).

`keep_position_cols`

:   Keep all columns of `positions` (default `TRUE`)? If `FALSE`, the result has the columns of `airr_df`, `x`, and `y`.

## Value

A data frame with the columns `x` and `y` added.

## See Also

[`readSpatialIdMapping()`](readSpatialIdMapping.md), [`extractSpatialIds()`](extractSpatialIds.md)

## Examples

``` R
reads <- data.frame(sequence_id = c("a", "b"), spatial_id_8um = c("s1", "s2"))
positions <- data.frame(
  barcode = c("s1", "s2"),
  pxl_col_in_fullres = c(100, 200),
  pxl_row_in_fullres = c(50, 60)
)
addTissuePositions(reads, positions)
```

functions.title: Add polygon IDs to a receptor table
functions.summary: `assignReceptorPolygons` adds polygon columns to a receptor table.
functions.markdown:
# assignReceptorPolygons

## Add polygon IDs to a receptor table

## Description

`assignReceptorPolygons` adds polygon columns to a receptor table. It keeps all rows.

## Usage

``` R
assignReceptorPolygons(
  receptors,
  object = NULL,
  polygon = NULL,
  column = "polygon_id",
  spatial_id = NULL,
  images = NULL,
  image_scale = NULL,
  swap_coords = NULL,
  polygon_val = NULL,
  x = "x",
  y = "y",
  receptor_x = "x",
  receptor_y = "y",
  polygon_id = "polygon",
  include_boundary = TRUE,
  slot = NULL
)
```

## Arguments

`receptors`

:   AIRR-style receptor table. You can give a SIRUP object here if you omit `object`.

`object`

:   Seurat object or SIRUP object.

`polygon`

:   Data frame of polygon vertices in order. It needs the columns set by `x` and `y`. If the column set by `polygon_id` exists, the function treats each polygon on its own. If `object` is a SIRUP object and `polygon` is `NULL`, the function uses the stored polygons.

`column`

:   Name of the column to add to the receptor table (default `"polygon_id"`).

`spatial_id`

:   Name of the `receptors` column that holds the spatial IDs. If `NULL`, the function uses the stored field of a SIRUP object, or looks for a standard spatial ID column.

`images`

:   Names of the Seurat images to use.

`image_scale`

:   Image scale for `SeuratObject::GetTissueCoordinates()`. If `NULL`, the function uses the value stored in the SIRUP object.

`swap_coords`

:   Swap the two Seurat coordinate axes? If `NULL`, the function uses the value stored in the SIRUP object. Give a value if `object` is a Seurat object.

`polygon_val`

:   IDs of the polygons to use. If `NULL`, the function uses all polygons.

`x`

:   Name of the x-coordinate column in `polygon` (default `"x"`).

`y`

:   Name of the y-coordinate column in `polygon` (default `"y"`).

`receptor_x`

:   Name of the x-coordinate column in `receptors`, for `object = NULL` (default `"x"`).

`receptor_y`

:   Name of the y-coordinate column in `receptors`, for `object = NULL` (default `"y"`).

`polygon_id`

:   Name of the column in `polygon` that groups the vertices by polygon (default `"polygon"`).

`include_boundary`

:   Count spots on a polygon edge as inside the polygon (default `TRUE`)?

`slot`

:   Name of the receptor slot to use. Leave it `NULL` if the SIRUP object has one receptor table. You must give it if the object has several slots. The function ignores `slot` if you give a plain receptor table.

## Details

If you give `object`, a receptor row gets `NA` if its spatial ID is outside the selected polygons or does not match the spatial object. If `object` is `NULL`, the function finds the polygons from the coordinate columns in `receptors`.

A row in overlapping polygons gets the smallest polygon by area in the primary column. The function also adds one logical column `⁠polygon_<ID>⁠` for each polygon. These columns show membership in every polygon.

If `receptors` is a SIRUP object and you omit `object` and `polygon`, the function uses the stored spatial object and polygons.

## Value

A tibble with the `column` added.

## See Also

[`assignSpatialPolygons()`](assignSpatialPolygons.md), [`withPolygons()`](withPolygons.md)

## Examples

``` R
x <- readSIRUP(system.file("extdata", "sirup_synthetic.rds", package = "SIRUP"))

# Use the spatial object and the polygons stored in the SIRUP object.
receptors <- assignReceptorPolygons(x)
table(receptors$polygon_id, useNA = "ifany")
```

functions.markdown:
# assignSpatialPolygons

## Add polygon IDs to the spatial metadata

## Description

`assignSpatialPolygons` adds polygon columns to the Seurat metadata. It keeps all spots.

## Usage

``` R
assignSpatialPolygons(
  object,
  polygon = NULL,
  images = NULL,
  image_scale = NULL,
  swap_coords = NULL,
  polygon_val = NULL,
  x = "x",
  y = "y",
  polygon_id = "polygon",
  metadata = "polygon_id",
  include_boundary = TRUE
)
```

## Arguments

`object`

:   Seurat object or SIRUP object.

`polygon`

:   Data frame of polygon vertices in order. It needs the columns set by `x` and `y`. If the column set by `polygon_id` exists, the function treats each polygon on its own. If `object` is a SIRUP object and `polygon` is `NULL`, the function uses the stored polygons.

`images`

:   Names of the Seurat images to use.

`image_scale`

:   Image scale for `SeuratObject::GetTissueCoordinates()`. If `NULL`, the function uses the value stored in the SIRUP object.

`swap_coords`

:   Swap the two Seurat coordinate axes? If `NULL`, the function uses the value stored in the SIRUP object. Give a value if `object` is a Seurat object.

`polygon_val`

:   IDs of the polygons to use. If `NULL`, the function uses all polygons.

`x`

:   Name of the x-coordinate column in `polygon` (default `"x"`).

`y`

:   Name of the y-coordinate column in `polygon` (default `"y"`).

`polygon_id`

:   Name of the column in `polygon` that groups the vertices by polygon (default `"polygon"`).

`metadata`

:   Name of the metadata column that holds the primary polygon of each spot (default `"polygon_id"`).

`include_boundary`

:   Count spots on a polygon edge as inside the polygon (default `TRUE`)?

## Details

A spot outside the selected polygons gets `NA` in the primary column. A spot in overlapping polygons gets the smallest polygon by area. The function also adds one logical column `⁠polygon_<ID>⁠` for each polygon. These columns show membership in every polygon.

## Value

A Seurat object with the `metadata` column added to `⁠@meta.data⁠`.

## See Also

[`seuratSubsetPolygon()`](seuratSubsetPolygon.md), [`assignReceptorPolygons()`](assignReceptorPolygons.md)

## Examples

``` R
x <- readSIRUP(system.file("extdata", "sirup_synthetic.rds", package = "SIRUP"))
flat <- data.frame(
  polygon = "block",
  x = c(3.5, 5.5, 5.5, 3.5),
  y = c(0.5, 0.5, 2.5, 2.5)
)
spatial <- assignSpatialPolygons(
  getSpatial(x),
  polygon = flat,
  image_scale = "hires",
  swap_coords = FALSE
)
table(spatial$polygon_id, useNA = "ifany")
```

functions.title: Assign colors to the tips of clones
functions.summary: `assignTipColors` gives each tip of each clone a color ID and a color.
functions.markdown:
# assignTipColors

## Assign colors to the tips of clones

## Description

`assignTipColors` gives each tip of each clone a color ID and a color. Tree plots and the matching spatial plots use the same colors.

## Usage

``` R
assignTipColors(
  clones,
  clone_val = NULL,
  clone = "clone_id",
  id = "sequence_id",
  shared_color = NULL,
  palette = NULL
)
```

## Arguments

`clones`

:   Data frame of AIRR data with clone IDs.

`clone_val`

:   Clone IDs to keep before the function assigns the colors. If `NULL`, the function keeps all clones.

`clone`

:   Name of the column that holds the clone IDs (default `"clone_id"`).

`id`

:   Name of the column that holds the sequence or tip IDs (default `"sequence_id"`).

`shared_color`

:   Name of a column. Tips that share a value in this column get the same color within a clone, for example a spatial ID column.

`palette`

:   Vector of colors. If `NULL`, the function uses `pals::glasbey()` if the package is installed. Otherwise, it uses the base R colors from `grDevices::hcl.colors()`.

## Details

The function numbers the tips of each clone in the order of `id`. If you give `shared_color`, tips with the same value of that column get the same number within a clone. For example, tips in the same spot get the same color.

## Value

A data frame with the columns `tip_color_id` and `tip_color` added.

## See Also

[`plotSpatialCloneTreePairs()`](plotSpatialCloneTreePairs.md)

## Examples

``` R
x <- readSIRUP(system.file("extdata", "sirup_synthetic.rds", package = "SIRUP"))
colors <- assignTipColors(getReceptors(x), shared_color = "spatial_id")
head(colors[, c("clone_id", "spatial_id", "tip_color_id", "tip_color")])
```

functions.title: Choose the number of tip clusters for a tree
functions.summary: `chooseTreeTipK` picks a number of tip clusters for one tree.
functions.markdown:
# chooseTreeTipK

## Choose the number of tip clusters for a tree

## Description

`chooseTreeTipK` picks a number of tip clusters for one tree.

## Usage

``` R
chooseTreeTipK(
  tree,
  k_range = 1:10,
  improvement_threshold = 0.1,
  ignore_tips = "Germline",
  method = c("cut_largest_branches", "split_largest_subtrees", "monophyletic_clades"),
  cut_terminal_edges = TRUE
)
```

## Arguments

`tree`

:   Phylogenetic tree with the fields `edge`, `edge.length`, and `tip.label`.

`k_range`

:   Values of `k` to test (default `1:10`).

`improvement_threshold`

:   Smallest relative improvement of the score that justifies a larger `k` (default 0.10).

`ignore_tips`

:   Tip labels to remove before the scoring (default `"Germline"`).

`method`

:   Clustering method for [`clusterTreeTips()`](clusterTreeTips.md). The default is `"cut_largest_branches"`.

`cut_terminal_edges`

:   Allow cuts of terminal branches (default `TRUE`)? The function passes the value to [`clusterTreeTips()`](clusterTreeTips.md).

## Details

For each value in `k_range`, the function runs [`clusterTreeTips()`](clusterTreeTips.md). It scores the result as the mean within cluster patristic distance. It finds the first `k` where the relative improvement of the score is below `improvement_threshold`, and picks the `k` before it. If the improvement never falls below the threshold, it picks the largest `k`.

## Value

A list with the chosen `k` and `scores`, a data frame with the columns `k`, `score`, and `relative_improvement`.

## See Also

[`clusterTreeTips()`](clusterTreeTips.md), [`clusterTreesTips()`](clusterTreesTips.md)

## Examples

``` R
x <- readSIRUP(system.file("extdata", "sirup_synthetic.rds", package = "SIRUP"))
x <- formatSpatialClones(
  x,
  id = "sequence_id",
  germ = "germline_alignment_d_mask",
  traits = "spatial_id"
)
x <- getSpatialTrees(x)
trees <- getAnalysis(x, "trees")
tree <- trees$trees[[1]]

chooseTreeTipK(tree)
```

functions.title: Cluster the tips of all trees in a dowser result
functions.summary: `clusterTreesTips` runs [`clusterTreeTips()`](clusterTreeTips.md) on each tree of a dowser result.
functions.markdown:
# clusterTreesTips

## Cluster the tips of all trees in a dowser result

## Description

`clusterTreesTips` runs [`clusterTreeTips()`](clusterTreeTips.md) on each tree of a dowser result. It adds the cluster column to the clone data of each tree.

## Usage

``` R
clusterTreesTips(
  trees,
  k = "auto",
  id = "sequence_id",
  cluster = "tree_cluster",
  prefix = "tree_cluster_",
  ignore_tips = "Germline",
  keep = NULL,
  keep_val = NULL,
  method = c("split_largest_subtrees", "cut_largest_branches", "monophyletic_clades"),
  cut_terminal_edges = FALSE,
  k_range = 1:8,
  improvement_threshold = 0.1
)
```

## Arguments

`trees`

:   Result of [`dowser::getTrees()`](https://dowser.readthedocs.io/en/latest/topics/getTrees/), or a list with an element `trees` that holds this result.

`k`

:   Number of subtrees to make in each tree. Use `"auto"` (default) to choose `k` for each tree with [`chooseTreeTipK()`](chooseTreeTipK.md).

`id`

:   Name of the column in each clone data frame that matches the tree tip labels (default `"sequence_id"`).

`cluster`

:   Name of the cluster column to add (default `"tree_cluster"`).

`prefix`

:   Prefix of the cluster labels (default `"tree_cluster_"`).

`ignore_tips`

:   Tip labels to remove before the clustering (default `"Germline"`).

`keep`

:   Name of a column in each clone data frame (default `NULL`). The function runs the clustering first. Then, for each tip where `keep` differs from `keep_val`, it replaces the cluster label with the value of `keep`.

`keep_val`

:   Value of `keep` that marks a tip to keep.

`method`

:   Clustering method for [`clusterTreeTips()`](clusterTreeTips.md). The default is `"split_largest_subtrees"`.

`cut_terminal_edges`

:   Allow cuts of terminal branches (default `FALSE`)? With `FALSE`, the function prefers internal splits of clades. With `TRUE`, branch cuts can remove single terminal tips.

`k_range`

:   Values of `k` to test, if `k = "auto"` (default `1:8`). The function passes it to [`chooseTreeTipK()`](chooseTreeTipK.md).

`improvement_threshold`

:   Smallest relative improvement that justifies a larger `k`, if `k = "auto"` (default 0.10). The function passes it to [`chooseTreeTipK()`](chooseTreeTipK.md).

## Value

`trees`, with the `cluster` column added to the clone data of each tree.

## See Also

[`clusterTreeTips()`](clusterTreeTips.md), [`chooseTreeTipK()`](chooseTreeTipK.md), [`plotSpatialCloneTreePairs()`](plotSpatialCloneTreePairs.md)

## Examples

``` R
x <- readSIRUP(system.file("extdata", "sirup_synthetic.rds", package = "SIRUP"))
x <- formatSpatialClones(
  x,
  id = "sequence_id",
  germ = "germline_alignment_d_mask",
  traits = "spatial_id"
)
x <- getSpatialTrees(x)
trees <- getAnalysis(x, "trees")
tree <- trees$trees[[1]]

# Use 3 clusters for every tree.
clustered <- clusterTreesTips(trees, k = 3)
table(clustered$data[[1]]@data$tree_cluster)

# Choose k for each tree.
clustered <- clusterTreesTips(trees, k = "auto")
```

functions.title: Cluster the tips of a tree
functions.summary: `clusterTreeTips` groups the tips of a phylogenetic tree into `k` connected clusters.
functions.markdown:
# clusterTreeTips

## Cluster the tips of a tree

## Description

`clusterTreeTips` groups the tips of a phylogenetic tree into `k` connected clusters.

## Usage

``` R
clusterTreeTips(
  tree,
  k,
  id = "sequence_id",
  cluster = "tree_cluster",
  ignore_tips = "Germline",
  prefix = "tree_cluster_",
  method = c("split_largest_subtrees", "cut_largest_branches", "monophyletic_clades"),
  cut_terminal_edges = TRUE
)
```

## Arguments

`tree`

:   Phylogenetic tree with the fields `edge`, `edge.length`, and `tip.label`.

`k`

:   Number of subtrees to make, before the function removes the ignored tips. If `k` is larger than the number of tips, the function gives a warning and uses the number of tips.

`id`

:   Name of the tip ID column in the result (default `"sequence_id"`).

`cluster`

:   Name of the cluster column in the result (default `"tree_cluster"`).

`ignore_tips`

:   Tip labels to remove **before** the clustering (default `"Germline"`). These tips do not form a cluster, do not use up a cluster, and do not appear in the result. The function always removes a tip named `"Germline"` (in any case). It prunes the tree with `ape::drop.tip()`. If `ape` is not installed, the function removes the tips from the result table after the clustering.

`prefix`

:   Prefix of the cluster labels (default `"tree_cluster_"`).

`method`

:   Clustering method: `"split_largest_subtrees"` (default), `"cut_largest_branches"`, or `"monophyletic_clades"`. See Details.

`cut_terminal_edges`

:   Allow cuts of terminal branches (default `TRUE`)? If `FALSE`, the function cuts internal branches first, so that it splits larger clades before it cuts off single tips.

## Details

The function groups the tips of the tree into `k` connected clusters. This helps with visualization: tips in the same cluster get the same label, and you can give them the same color. Each cluster is a subtree. The function makes the `k` subtrees by cutting `k - 1` branches. The `method` argument sets how the function chooses the branches to cut:

- `split_largest_subtrees` (default): The function splits one subtree at each step. It picks the subtree with the largest genetic span, which is the largest patristic distance between two of its tips. If two subtrees tie, it picks the subtree with more tips. In that subtree, a candidate branch must leave two subtrees that each have at least one tip. The function cuts the branch that makes the smaller of the two subtrees as large as possible (by tip count). If branches tie, it cuts the longest branch. If `cut_terminal_edges` is `FALSE`, the function considers internal branches first. It considers terminal branches (the branches that end in a tip) only if no internal branch is valid. This stops the function from cutting off long terminal branches before it splits the larger clades. The function stops after `k - 1` cuts, or when no valid cut remains.

- `cut_largest_branches`: The function cuts the `k - 1` longest branches of the whole tree. If `cut_terminal_edges` is `FALSE`, it cuts the longest internal branches first. It cuts terminal branches only if the tree has fewer than `k - 1` internal branches. This is the heuristic for fixed-k minimum spanning tree clustering, applied to a phylogenetic tree.

- `monophyletic_clades`: Each cluster is one complete clade, which is a node and all of its descendants. No cluster is a paraphyletic remainder. Use this method if each cluster must match a real clade, for example if each tip color in a figure must mark one monophyletic group. The function starts with the whole tree as one clade. At each step it picks the clade with the largest genetic span (the clade needs at least two tips). It replaces that clade with all of its child clades, which are the subtrees that start at the children of its root node. The function stops when `k` clades exist, or when no clade can split. `cut_terminal_edges` has no effect. For a bifurcating tree, the result has exactly `k` clades. At a multifurcation, one step adds all child clades, so the result can have more than `k` clades. If an ignored tip (such as the germline) forms its own clade, the function removes that clade. The result can then have fewer than `k` clusters.

The function labels the clusters with `prefix` and a number, such as `tree_cluster_1`.

## Value

A data frame with one row for each kept tip. It has the tip ID column (named by `id`) and the cluster label column (named by `cluster`).

## See Also

[`chooseTreeTipK()`](chooseTreeTipK.md), [`clusterTreesTips()`](clusterTreesTips.md)

## Examples

``` R
x <- readSIRUP(system.file("extdata", "sirup_synthetic.rds", package = "SIRUP"))
x <- formatSpatialClones(
  x,
  id = "sequence_id",
  germ = "germline_alignment_d_mask",
  traits = "spatial_id"
)
x <- getSpatialTrees(x)
trees <- getAnalysis(x, "trees")
tree <- trees$trees[[1]]

# Cut the tree into 3 clusters.
clusterTreeTips(tree, k = 3)

# Make each cluster one complete clade.
clusterTreeTips(tree, k = 3, method = "monophyletic_clades")
```

functions.title: Collapse neighboring spots with identical receptor sequences
functions.summary: `collapseIdenticalNeighbors` finds groups of neighboring spots that share a receptor sequence.
functions.markdown:
# collapseIdenticalNeighbors

## Collapse neighboring spots with identical receptor sequences

## Description

`collapseIdenticalNeighbors` finds groups of neighboring spots that share a receptor sequence. It keeps one representative spot for each group.

## Usage

``` R
collapseIdenticalNeighbors(
  object,
  seurat_object = NULL,
  spatial_id = NULL,
  sequence = "sequence",
  consensus_count = "consensus_count",
  images = NULL,
  image_scale = NULL,
  swap_coords = NULL,
  num_neighbors_non_boundary = 6L,
  slot = NULL,
  validate = TRUE
)
```

## Arguments

`object`

:   SIRUP object, or an AIRR-style receptor data frame.

`seurat_object`

:   Seurat object. Use it only if `object` is a receptor data frame.

`spatial_id`

:   Name of the receptor column that holds the Seurat spot names. For a SIRUP object, if you omit it, the function uses the stored spatial ID field. For a receptor table, if you omit it, the function looks for a standard spatial ID column.

`sequence`

:   Name of the column that holds the receptor sequences (default `"sequence"`).

`consensus_count`

:   Name of the column that holds the consensus counts (default `"consensus_count"`). The function uses it to choose the representative spot of a group.

`images`

:   Names of the Seurat images to use for the coordinates.

`image_scale`

:   Image scale for `SeuratObject::GetTissueCoordinates()`.

`swap_coords`

:   Swap the x and y coordinates after the function reads the Seurat coordinates?

`num_neighbors_non_boundary`

:   Number of nearby spots that makes a spot a non-boundary spot (default 6).

`slot`

:   Name of the receptor slot to collapse if `object` is a SIRUP object. Leave it `NULL` if the object has one receptor table. You must give it if the object has several slots. The function changes only that slot.

`validate`

:   Validate the updated SIRUP object (default `TRUE`)? The function uses it only if `object` is a SIRUP object.

## Details

For each unique receptor sequence, the function finds the connected groups of neighboring spots that hold that sequence. It keeps the spot with the highest consensus count in each group. This hopefully reduces bleedover, but in a very coarse manner.

## Value

For a SIRUP object, the updated SIRUP object with a new receptor table. For a receptor table, the collapsed table. Both keep only the representative spot of each group of identical sequences.

## See Also

[`filterAirr()`](filterAirr.md), [`updateReceptors()`](sirup-transform.md)

functions.title: Keep the most abundant consensus sequence of each spatial ID and locus
functions.summary: `collapseTopConsensusPerSpatialId` keeps the row with the highest consensus count for each spatial ID and locus.
functions.markdown:
# collapseTopConsensusPerSpatialId

## Keep the most abundant consensus sequence of each spatial ID and locus

## Description

`collapseTopConsensusPerSpatialId` keeps the row with the highest consensus count for each spatial ID and locus.

## Usage

``` R
collapseTopConsensusPerSpatialId(
  airr_df,
  spatial_id = "spatial_id_2um",
  locus = "locus",
  consensus = "consensus_count",
  sequence = "sequence",
  alignment = "sequence_alignment",
  ties = c("all", "first")
)
```

## Arguments

`airr_df`

:   AIRR-style data frame.

`spatial_id`

:   Name of the spatial ID column for the grouping (default `"spatial_id_2um"`).

`locus`

:   Name of the locus column for the grouping (default `"locus"`).

`consensus`

:   Name of the consensus count column for the ranking (default `"consensus_count"`).

`sequence`

:   Name of the sequence column for the proportion of called bases (default `"sequence"`).

`alignment`

:   Name of the alignment column for the gap measures (default `"sequence_alignment"`).

`ties`

:   Keep `"all"` rows that tie for the top count (default), or only the `"first"` of them.

## Details

The function adds the column `prop_total_consensus`. It then adds the quality columns from [`addSequenceQualityMetrics()`](addSequenceQualityMetrics.md): `non_N_nucleotide_prop`, `max_gap_length`, and `opening_gap_length`. If several rows tie for the top consensus count, the function prints how many groups have a tie.

## Value

The collapsed data frame. It has the column `prop_total_consensus` (the count of the row divided by the total count of its group) and the quality columns.

## See Also

[`addSequenceQualityMetrics()`](addSequenceQualityMetrics.md), [`filterAirr()`](filterAirr.md)

## Examples

``` R
x <- readSIRUP(system.file("extdata", "sirup_synthetic.rds", package = "SIRUP"))
collapseTopConsensusPerSpatialId(getReceptors(x), spatial_id = "spatial_id")
```

functions.title: Create a SIRUP object
functions.summary: `createSIRUP` joins a Seurat spatial object and an AIRR receptor table into one SIRUP object.
functions.markdown:
# createSIRUP

## Create a SIRUP object

## Description

`createSIRUP` joins a Seurat spatial object and an AIRR receptor table into one SIRUP object.

## Usage

``` R
createSIRUP(
  spatial,
  receptors,
  spatial_id = NULL,
  image = NULL,
  sample_id = NULL,
  clone = NULL,
  locus = "locus",
  count = NULL,
  image_scale = NULL,
  swap_coords = NULL,
  metadata = list(),
  polygons = NULL,
  polygons_path = NULL,
  include_boundary = TRUE,
  analyses = list(),
  validate = TRUE
)
```

## Arguments

`spatial`

:   Seurat object with spatial expression data, or a named list of Seurat objects (one per spatial sample).

`receptors`

:   AIRR-style receptor table (a data frame or similar), or a named list of such tables. Each table in a list is one slot, for example `list(bcr = bcr_table, tcr = tcr_table)`.

`spatial_id`

:   Name of the `receptors` column that holds the spatial cell or spot IDs. If `NULL`, the function uses the first column found from this list: `spatial_id`, `spatial_id_8um`, `spatial_id_2um`, `spatial_id_16um`, `barcode_8um`, `barcode_2um`, `cell`, `cell_barcode`. It stores the name in the metadata and gives an error if none exists.

`image`

:   Name of the `receptors` column that identifies the Seurat image (default `NULL`).

`sample_id`

:   Name of the `receptors` column that holds the sample name. If `spatial` is a named list, this argument is required. If a Seurat object has no such metadata column, the function fills it with the list name.

`clone`

:   Name of the `receptors` column that holds the clone ID (default `NULL`). The function gives an error if the column does not exist.

`locus`

:   Name of the `receptors` column that holds the receptor locus (default `"locus"`). If you use the default and the column does not exist, the function stores `NULL`. If you give another name that does not exist, the function gives an error.

`count`

:   Name of the `receptors` column that holds the observation count or weight (default `NULL`).

`image_scale`

:   Default Seurat image scale (default `NULL`). Plotting and spatial statistics functions use it when their own `image_scale` is `NULL`. For multi-sample objects, give a named vector or list with one value for each sample, or one unnamed value that applies to all samples.

`swap_coords`

:   Swap the two Seurat coordinate axes by default (default `NULL`)? Plotting and spatial statistics functions use this value when their own `swap_coords` is `NULL`. For multi-sample objects, give a named vector or list with one value for each sample, or one unnamed value that applies to all samples.

`metadata`

:   Named list of dataset-level metadata.

`polygons`

:   Polygon table (default `NULL`). The table has one row per polygon, with a `polygon_id` column and a list column `vertices`. Each `vertices` table needs columns `x` and `y`. It can also have `spatial_id` and `image`. The function adds a `polygon_id` column and one logical `⁠polygon_<ID>⁠` column per polygon to both the Seurat metadata and the receptor table.

`polygons_path`

:   Path to a flat CSV file of polygon vertices (default `NULL`). The file needs `x` and `y` columns and a `polygon_id` or `polygon` column. The function annotates these polygons in the same way as `polygons`.

`include_boundary`

:   Count spots on a polygon edge as members of the polygon (default `TRUE`)?

`analyses`

:   Named list of derived analysis results.

`validate`

:   Validate the new object (default `TRUE`)?

## Details

`spatial` can be one Seurat object or a named list of Seurat objects. If you give a list, the column of `receptors` that `sample_id` names must name the corresponding list entry for each row. The function keeps rows with no matching entry as nonspatial records. For example, these rows can hold bulk or single-cell data.

The function stores key receptor column names in `metadata$receptor_fields` and converts `receptors` to a [`tibble::tibble()`](https://tibble.tidyverse.org/reference/tibble.html). The optional `analyses` list keeps derived results.

`receptors` can also be a named list of tables, for example one table of BCRs and one of TCRs. Each table is a *slot*. All slots share the same spatial data, polygons and field mappings. The spatial ID and sample columns must be in every table. Each other mapped column, such as `clone_id`, must be in at least one table. Clone IDs only need to be unique within one slot. Functions that use receptors analyse one slot at a time, chosen with their `slot` argument. A SIRUP object with one table has the slot name `"only_slot"`.

The examples in this package use a small synthetic SIRUP object. It has 25 spots, 10 genes, 5 clones, and 2 polygons. The spots and gene counts are simulated. The receptor rows are real BCR sequences from a human thymus section, assigned to synthetic spots. Load the object with `readSIRUP(system.file("extdata", "sirup_synthetic.rds", package = "SIRUP"))`. The script `data-raw/make_synthetic_example.R` builds it.

## Value

A SIRUP object (S3 class `sirup`).

## See Also

[`validateSIRUP()`](validateSIRUP.md), [`mergeSIRUP()`](mergeSIRUP.md), [`saveSIRUP()`](sirup-io.md)

## Examples

``` R
# Use the small synthetic object that comes with the package.
x <- readSIRUP(system.file("extdata", "sirup_synthetic.rds", package = "SIRUP"))
x

# Build a SIRUP object from a Seurat object and a receptor table.
sirup <- createSIRUP(
  spatial = getSpatial(x),
  receptors = getReceptors(x),
  spatial_id = "spatial_id",
  clone = "clone_id",
  image_scale = "hires",
  swap_coords = FALSE
)
sirup
```

functions.title: Download the SIRUP example data
functions.summary: Download the myasthenia gravis (MG) thymus example files that the guides on the SIRUP website use.
functions.markdown:
# downloadSIRUPExample

## Download the SIRUP example data

## Description

Download the myasthenia gravis (MG) thymus example files that the guides on the SIRUP website use. The files are not part of the package, to keep the package small. The function skips files that are already in `dest` and checks every download against a stored MD5 sum.

## Usage

``` R
downloadSIRUPExample(
  dest = file.path(tempdir(), "SIRUP_example"),
  files = NULL,
  overwrite = FALSE,
  base_url = getOption("SIRUP.example_url", .sirup_example_url),
  quiet = FALSE
)
```

## Arguments

`dest`

: Folder to save the files in. The function creates it if needed. The default is a folder in the R session\'s temporary directory, so the files are lost when you close R. Give a permanent folder to keep them.

`files`

: Names of the files to download. If `NULL` (default), the function downloads all files. Use this to download only what a guide needs.

`overwrite`

: Download a file again even if it is already in `dest` (default `FALSE`)?

`base_url`

: Web address of the folder that holds the files. Change it only to use a mirror. A `⁠file://⁠` address of a local folder also works. The default is the option `SIRUP.example_url` if you set it.

`quiet`

: Hide the download progress messages (default `FALSE`)?

## Details

The files are:

- `mg_thymus_slice1_spatial.rds`, `mg_thymus_slice2_spatial.rds`: spatial Seurat objects for the two tissue sections.

- `mg_thymus_slice1_bcr.tsv.gz`, `mg_thymus_slice2_bcr.tsv.gz`: AIRR rearrangement tables of IGH sequences with spatial IDs.

- `mg_thymus_slice2_tcr.tsv.gz`, `mg_thymus_slice2_reads.tsv.gz`: TCR sequences and the demultiplexed reads of section 2.

- `mg_thymus_slice1_gc_polygons.csv`, `mg_thymus_slice2_gc_polygons.csv`: annotated polygons of the ectopic germinal centers.

- `mg_thymus_cell_types.csv.gz`: cell-type proportions for each spot.

- `mg_thymus_bulk_*.tsv.gz`: bulk repertoire tables from thymus and blood.

## Value

The path of `dest`, invisibly. Use `file.path()` with the path and a file name to read a file.

## See Also

[`readSIRUP()`](sirup-io.md)

## Examples

``` R

extdata <- downloadSIRUPExample(
  files = c("mg_thymus_slice2_spatial.rds", "mg_thymus_slice2_bcr.tsv.gz")
)
thymus <- readRDS(file.path(extdata, "mg_thymus_slice2_spatial.rds"))
```

functions.title: Expand polygons outward from their centroids
functions.summary: `expandPolygons` makes each polygon larger by moving its vertices away from the polygon centroid.
functions.markdown:
# expandPolygons

## Expand polygons outward from their centroids

## Description

`expandPolygons` makes each polygon larger by moving its vertices away from the polygon centroid.

## Usage

``` R
expandPolygons(
  polygons,
  delta = NULL,
  x = "x",
  y = "y",
  polygon_id = "polygon"
)
```

## Arguments

`polygons`

:   Polygons to expand. Give a flat data frame of vertices (with `x`, `y`, and, if you want, a polygon ID column). You can also pass a SIRUP object. The function then expands the stored polygons.

`delta`

:   Distance that each vertex moves outward, in coordinate units. Required. A negative value moves the vertices inward, so the polygon becomes smaller.

`x`

:   Name of the x-coordinate column, if `polygons` is a data frame (default `"x"`).

`y`

:   Name of the y-coordinate column, if `polygons` is a data frame (default `"y"`).

`polygon_id`

:   Name of the column that separates the polygons, if `polygons` is a data frame (default `"polygon"`). If the column does not exist, the function uses a `polygon` or `polygon_id` column. If neither exists, all rows form one polygon.

## Details

Each vertex moves along the line from the centroid through the vertex. It moves by the distance `delta`. The polygon keeps its shape and its number of vertices. The polygons must be convex.

## Value

The expanded polygons in the form of the input: a data frame for a data frame, or the updated SIRUP object for a SIRUP object.

## See Also

[`addPolygons()`](sirup-polygons.md), [`plotSpatialPolygons()`](plotSpatialPolygons.md)

## Examples

``` R
x <- readSIRUP(system.file("extdata", "sirup_synthetic.rds", package = "SIRUP"))

# Make the stored polygons larger by 0.25 coordinate units.
x2 <- expandPolygons(x, delta = 0.25)

# Use a data frame of vertices.
flat <- data.frame(
  polygon = "block",
  x = c(3.5, 5.5, 5.5, 3.5),
  y = c(0.5, 0.5, 2.5, 2.5)
)
expandPolygons(flat, delta = 0.25)
```

functions.title: Extract spatial IDs from sequence IDs
functions.summary: `extractSpatialIds` copies the spatial ID out of the sequence ID with a regular expression.
functions.markdown:
# extractSpatialIds

## Extract spatial IDs from sequence IDs

## Description

`extractSpatialIds` copies the spatial ID out of the sequence ID with a regular expression. It adds the spatial ID as a column.

## Usage

``` R
extractSpatialIds(
  airr_df,
  id = "sequence_id",
  spatial_id = "spatial_id",
  regex,
  prefix = "",
  suffix = ""
)
```

## Arguments

`airr_df`

:   AIRR-style data frame.

`id`

:   Name of the column that holds the read or consensus IDs (default `"sequence_id"`).

`spatial_id`

:   Name of the new spatial ID column (default `"spatial_id"`).

`regex`

:   Regular expression that matches the spatial ID. If it has a capture group, the function uses the first group. Otherwise, it uses the whole match.

`prefix`

:   Text to add before the match (default `""`).

`suffix`

:   Text to add after the match (default `""`).

## Value

`airr_df` with the `spatial_id` column added. A row with no match gets `NA`.

## See Also

[`parseRadSequenceIds()`](parseRadSequenceIds.md), [`addTissuePositions()`](addTissuePositions.md)

## Examples

``` R
reads <- data.frame(
  sequence_id = c("consensus1,ACGTACGTACGTACGT", "consensus2,TTTTGGGGCCCCAAAA")
)

# Take the 16-nucleotide barcode and add the suffix of the Seurat spot names.
extractSpatialIds(reads, regex = ",([ACGT]{16})$", suffix = "-1")
```

functions.title: Filter AIRR sequences
functions.summary: `filterAirr` filters sequences from an AIRR table.
functions.markdown:
# filterAirr

## Filter AIRR sequences

## Description

`filterAirr` filters sequences from an AIRR table. \]

## Usage

``` R
filterAirr(
  airr_df,
  locus_val = NULL,
  min_v_length = 100,
  min_j_length = 10,
  min_junction_length = 1,
  productive_only = TRUE,
  complete_vdj = FALSE,
  min_consensus_count = 2,
  max_opening_gap = NULL,
  max_gap_length = NULL,
  sequence_alignment = "sequence_alignment",
  id = "sequence_id",
  spatial_id = NULL,
  add_spatial_sequence_id = FALSE,
  spatial_sequence_id = "spatial_sequence_id",
  spatial_id_key = "spatial_id"
)
```

## Arguments

`airr_df`

:   AIRR-style data frame. It needs the columns `v_sequence_start`, `v_sequence_end`, `j_sequence_start`, `j_sequence_end`, and `junction_length`.

`locus_val`

:   Loci to keep. If `NULL` (default), the function does not filter by locus.

`min_v_length`

:   Smallest V length to keep (default 100).

`min_j_length`

:   Smallest J length to keep (default 10).

`min_junction_length`

:   Smallest junction length to keep (default 1).

`productive_only`

:   Keep only productive rearrangements (default `TRUE`)?

`complete_vdj`

:   Keep only rows with a complete V(D)J (default `FALSE`)? IgBLAST writes this column as `"T"` or `"F"`. The function skips the filter if the column does not exist.

`min_consensus_count`

:   Smallest `consensus_count` to keep (default 2). Use `NULL` to skip the filter.

`max_opening_gap`

:   Longest gap at the start of `sequence_alignment` to keep. If `NULL` (default), the function does not filter by this gap.

`max_gap_length`

:   Longest run of gap characters in `sequence_alignment` to keep. If `NULL` (default), the function does not filter by this gap. A real somatic hypermutation indel has a length that is a multiple of three. It is rarely longer than 12 nucleotides. A longer gap points to a chimeric or truncated consensus. The function measures the gap in the IMGT-numbered alignment. In this alignment, the padding depends on the locus: IGHV has padding of 6, 9, or 12 nucleotides, and TRBV has padding of 18 or 21. A limit that suits IGH rejects every TRB sequence, so set the limit for each locus.

`sequence_alignment`

:   Name of the alignment column for the gap filters (default `"sequence_alignment"`).

`id`

:   Name of the column that holds the read or consensus IDs (default `"sequence_id"`).

`spatial_id`

:   Name of a spatial ID column that exists in `airr_df`.

`add_spatial_sequence_id`

:   Add a column that combines the sequence ID and the spatial ID (default `FALSE`)? You must give `spatial_id` if you use `TRUE`.

`spatial_sequence_id`

:   Name of the combined column (default `"spatial_sequence_id"`).

`spatial_id_key`

:   Field name for the spatial ID in the combined column (default `"spatial_id"`). A value looks like `⁠sequence_id=<id>|<key>=<spatial ID>⁠`.

## Details

The function keeps the rows that pass all of these filters. It skips a filter if its column is missing, unless you set the argument yourself. In that case, it gives a warning.

- the locus (`locus_val`);

- the V length, J length, and junction length (`min_v_length`, `min_j_length`, `min_junction_length`);

- productive rearrangements (`productive_only`);

- complete V(D)J rearrangements (`complete_vdj`);

- the consensus count (`min_consensus_count`);

- the gap lengths in `sequence_alignment` (`max_opening_gap`, `max_gap_length`).

The function prints the number of rows that it kept.

## Value

The filtered data frame. It has the added columns `v_sequence_length` and `j_sequence_length`, and the combined ID column if you asked for it.

## See Also

[`addSequenceQualityMetrics()`](addSequenceQualityMetrics.md), [`plotLengthQc()`](plotLengthQc.md), [`processSpatialSample()`](processSpatialSample.md)

## Examples

``` R
x <- readSIRUP(system.file("extdata", "sirup_synthetic.rds", package = "SIRUP"))
receptors <- getReceptors(x)

# The thresholds of the SIRUP paper.
filterAirr(
  receptors,
  locus_val = "IGH",
  min_v_length = 250,
  min_j_length = 30,
  min_junction_length = 10
)
```

functions.title: Format the receptors of a SIRUP object as in dowser's formatClones()
functions.summary: `formatSpatialClones` runs [`dowser::formatClones()`](https://dowser.readthedocs.io/en/latest/topics/formatClones/) on the receptor table of a SIRUP object.
functions.markdown:
# formatSpatialClones

## Format the receptors of a SIRUP object as in dowser\'s `formatClones()`

## Description

`formatSpatialClones` runs [`dowser::formatClones()`](https://dowser.readthedocs.io/en/latest/topics/formatClones/) on the receptor table of a SIRUP object. It stores the result as an analysis.

## Usage

``` R
formatSpatialClones(
  object,
  analysis_name = NULL,
  seq = "sequence_alignment",
  clone = "clone_id",
  subgroup = "clone_subgroup",
  id = "sequence_id",
  germ = "germline_alignment_d_mask",
  v_call = "v_call",
  j_call = "j_call",
  junc_len = "junction_length",
  mask_char = "N",
  max_mask = 0,
  pad_end = TRUE,
  text_fields = NULL,
  num_fields = NULL,
  seq_fields = NULL,
  add_count = TRUE,
  verbose = FALSE,
  collapse = TRUE,
  cell = "cell_id",
  locus = "locus",
  traits = NULL,
  mod3 = TRUE,
  randomize = TRUE,
  use_regions = TRUE,
  dup_singles = FALSE,
  nproc = 1,
  chain = "H",
  heavy = "IGH",
  filterstop = TRUE,
  minseq = 2,
  split_light = FALSE,
  light_traits = FALSE,
  majoronly = FALSE,
  columns = NULL,
  slot = NULL,
  validate = TRUE
)
```

## Arguments

`object`

:   A SIRUP object.

`analysis_name`

:   Name for the stored formatted clones (default `"f_clones"`). If the object has several receptor slots, the default also ends with `⁠_⁠` and the slot name.

`seq`

:   Name of the column that holds the observed DNA sequences (default `"sequence_alignment"`). The sequences must be aligned to each other.

`clone`

:   Name of the column that holds the clone ID (default `"clone_id"`).

`subgroup`

:   Name of the column that holds the subgroup ID (default `"clone_subgroup"`).

`id`

:   Name of the column that holds the sequence IDs (default `"sequence_id"`).

`germ`

:   Name of the column that holds the germline DNA sequences (default `"germline_alignment_d_mask"`). Each clone must have one germline. It must be aligned to the sequences in `seq`.

`v_call`

:   Name of the column that holds the V-segment alleles (default `"v_call"`). Within a clone, the entries must be the same at the gene level.

`j_call`

:   Name of the column that holds the J-segment alleles (default `"j_call"`). Within a clone, the entries must be the same at the gene level.

`junc_len`

:   Name of the numeric column that holds the junction length (default `"junction_length"`). Within a clone, the entries must be the same.

`mask_char`

:   Character for masking and padding (default `"N"`).

`max_mask`

:   Largest number of characters to mask at the start and at the end of the sequences (default 0). With `0`, the function does not mask. With `NULL`, the function uses the largest number of leading or trailing Ns in the sequences.

`pad_end`

:   Pad the end of each sequence with `mask_char` so that all sequences have the same length (default `TRUE`)?

`text_fields`

:   Names of the text columns to keep and merge when the function removes duplicates.

`num_fields`

:   Names of the numeric columns to keep and sum when the function removes duplicates.

`seq_fields`

:   Names of the sequence columns to keep and collapse when the function removes duplicates. Do not repeat `seq` or `germ` here.

`add_count`

:   Add the column `COLLAPSE_COUNT`, which holds the number of sequences that the function collapsed (default `TRUE`)?

`verbose`

:   Report the numbers of input, dropped, and output sequences (default `FALSE`)? The function passes it to `collapseDuplicates`.

`collapse`

:   Collapse identical sequences (default `TRUE`)?

`cell`

:   Name of the column that holds the cell IDs (default `"cell_id"`).

`locus`

:   Name of the column that holds the locus (default `"locus"`).

`traits`

:   Names of the columns to keep separate when the function collapses sequences. Include the spatial ID column if you want to plot the tips on the tissue.

`mod3`

:   Pad the sequences to a length that is a multiple of three (default `TRUE`)?

`randomize`

:   Put the sequences in random order (default `TRUE`)? This is important for PHYLIP.

`use_regions`

:   Assign the CDR and FWR regions (default `TRUE`)?

`dup_singles`

:   Duplicate the sequence of a clone that has one sequence, so that the clone gives a tree (default `FALSE`)?

`nproc`

:   Number of cores for the formatting (default 1).

`chain`

:   Use `"HL"` to include the light chain, if it exists. The default is `"H"`.

`heavy`

:   Name of the heavy chain locus (default `"IGH"`).

`filterstop`

:   Use only sequences with no in-frame stop codon (default `TRUE`)?

`minseq`

:   Smallest number of sequences in a clone (default 2).

`split_light`

:   Split the subgroups, or lump them together (default `FALSE`)? See `resolveLightChains` in dowser.

`light_traits`

:   Include the traits of the light chain when the function joins and collapses the sequences (default `FALSE`)?

`majoronly`

:   Return only the largest subgroup and the sequences with no light chain (default `FALSE`)?

`columns`

:   Names of other columns to keep in the result.

`slot`

:   Name of the receptor slot to use. Leave it `NULL` if the SIRUP object has one receptor table. You must give it if the object has several slots.

`validate`

:   Validate the updated SIRUP object (default `TRUE`)?

## Details

The function puts clones into a standardized format for downstream analysis. See [`dowser::formatClones()`](https://dowser.readthedocs.io/en/latest/topics/formatClones/) for details. The function stores the result as an analysis in the SIRUP object. The default analysis name is `"f_clones"`.

[`dowser::formatClones()`](https://dowser.readthedocs.io/en/latest/topics/formatClones/) takes a data frame and returns a tibble of `airrClone` objects. `formatSpatialClones` calls it with the receptor table of a SIRUP object and adds four things that spatial analysis needs: This function automatically does not collapse identical sequences across distinct samples. To plot the tips on the tissue, add the spatial ID column to `traits`.

## Value

The updated SIRUP object, with the formatted clones as an analysis.

## See Also

[`getSpatialTrees()`](getSpatialTrees.md), [`dowser::formatClones()`](https://dowser.readthedocs.io/en/latest/topics/formatClones/)

## Examples

``` R
x <- readSIRUP(system.file("extdata", "sirup_synthetic.rds", package = "SIRUP"))
x <- formatSpatialClones(
  x,
  id = "sequence_id",
  germ = "germline_alignment_d_mask",
  traits = "spatial_id"
)
getAnalysis(x, "f_clones")
```

functions.title: Format point sets as polygon vertices
functions.summary: `formatSpatialPolygons` converts a table of points into the vertex table that [`selectSpatialPolygons()`](selectSpatialPolygons.md) returns.
functions.markdown:
# formatSpatialPolygons

## Format point sets as polygon vertices

## Description

`formatSpatialPolygons` converts a table of points into the vertex table that [`selectSpatialPolygons()`](selectSpatialPolygons.md) returns.

## Usage

``` R
formatSpatialPolygons(
  object,
  polygon_points,
  spatial_id = "spatial_id",
  polygon = "polygon",
  x = "x",
  y = "y",
  image = "image",
  point_type = c("interior", "boundary"),
  buffer_radius = NULL,
  order = NULL,
  images = NULL,
  image_scale = NULL,
  swap_coords = NULL,
  close_polygons = TRUE
)
```

## Arguments

`object`

:   Seurat object or SIRUP object.

`polygon_points`

:   Data frame of points. With `point_type = "interior"`, it holds all points inside each polygon. With `point_type = "boundary"`, it holds the boundary points.

`spatial_id`

:   Name of the column in `polygon_points` that holds the spatial IDs (default `"spatial_id"`). You need it if `polygon_points` has no `x` and `y` columns.

`polygon`

:   Name of the column in `polygon_points` that identifies the polygons (default `"polygon"`).

`x`

:   Name of the x-coordinate column in `polygon_points`, if it exists (default `"x"`).

`y`

:   Name of the y-coordinate column in `polygon_points`, if it exists (default `"y"`).

`image`

:   Name of the image column in `polygon_points`, if it exists (default `"image"`).

`point_type`

:   Type of the points in `polygon_points`: `interior` (all points inside) or `boundary`.

`buffer_radius`

:   Radius for the buffer around the points. If `NULL`, the function estimates it from the spacing between nearest neighbors in the full coordinate grid.

`order`

:   Name of a column that orders the points in each polygon. It is most useful with `point_type = "boundary"`.

`images`

:   Names of the Seurat images to use.

`image_scale`

:   Image scale for `SeuratObject::GetTissueCoordinates()`. If `NULL`, the function uses the value stored in the SIRUP object.

`swap_coords`

:   Swap the two Seurat coordinate axes? If `NULL`, the function uses the value stored in the SIRUP object.

`close_polygons`

:   Close each polygon by repeating the first vertex, if needed (default `TRUE`)?

## Details

By default, `polygon_points` holds all points inside each polygon. The function merges the points with `sf`. Then it maps the outer ring back to the nearest selected spatial ID coordinates. The boundary keeps a valid order for concave polygons, and the vertices are spatial ID coordinates. If the input already holds boundary points, use `point_type = "boundary"`.

## Value

A data frame with the columns `spatial_id`, `x`, `y`, `polygon`, and `image`. The function drops polygons with fewer than three points and gives a warning.

## See Also

[`selectSpatialPolygons()`](selectSpatialPolygons.md), [`addPolygons()`](sirup-polygons.md)

## Examples

``` R
x <- readSIRUP(system.file("extdata", "sirup_synthetic.rds", package = "SIRUP"))

# Four spots that lie inside one polygon.
points <- data.frame(
  spatial_id = c("spot04", "spot05", "spot09", "spot10"),
  polygon = "block"
)
formatSpatialPolygons(x, points, image_scale = "hires", swap_coords = FALSE)
```

functions.title: Build trees from the formatted clones of a SIRUP object
functions.summary: `getSpatialTrees` runs [`dowser::getTrees()`](https://dowser.readthedocs.io/en/latest/topics/getTrees/) on the stored formatted clones.
functions.markdown:
# getSpatialTrees

## Build trees from the formatted clones of a SIRUP object

## Description

`getSpatialTrees` runs [`dowser::getTrees()`](https://dowser.readthedocs.io/en/latest/topics/getTrees/) on the stored formatted clones. It stores the trees as an analysis.

## Usage

``` R
getSpatialTrees(
  object,
  f_clones_analysis = NULL,
  analysis_name = NULL,
  trait = NULL,
  id = NULL,
  dir = NULL,
  modelfile = NULL,
  build = "pratchet",
  exec = NULL,
  igphyml = NULL,
  fixtrees = FALSE,
  nproc = 1,
  quiet = 0,
  rm_temp = TRUE,
  palette = NULL,
  seq = NULL,
  collapse = FALSE,
  check_divergence = TRUE,
  ...,
  slot = NULL,
  validate = TRUE
)
```

## Arguments

`object`

:   A SIRUP object.

`f_clones_analysis`

:   Name of the stored formatted clones. If `NULL`, the function uses `"f_clones"`, or `"f_clones_<slot>"` if the object has several receptor slots.

`analysis_name`

:   Name for the stored trees (default `"trees"`). If the object has several receptor slots, the default also ends with `⁠_⁠` and the slot name.

`trait`

:   Trait for the parsimony models. You need it if you use `igphyml`.

`id`

:   Unique name for this analysis. You need it if you use `igphyml` or `dnapars`.

`dir`

:   Directory for the temporary files.

`modelfile`

:   File that sets the parsimony model.

`build`

:   Program that builds the trees: `pratchet` (default), `pml`, `dnapars`, `dnaml`, `igphyml`, or `raxml`.

`exec`

:   Location of the phylogenetic program.

`igphyml`

:   Location of the `igphyml` program, for parsimony.

`fixtrees`

:   Use the tree topologies that you supply (default `FALSE`)?

`nproc`

:   Number of cores for the calculations (default 1).

`quiet`

:   Amount of text that the function prints to the console (default 0).

`rm_temp`

:   Delete the temporary files (default `TRUE`)?

`palette`

:   Deprecated.

`seq`

:   Name of the column that holds the sequences.

`collapse`

:   Collapse the internal nodes that have identical sequences (default `FALSE`)?

`check_divergence`

:   Run `checkDivergence` on the trees (default `TRUE`)?

`...`

:   Other arguments for the tree-building programs.

`slot`

:   Name of the receptor slot that the trees come from. The function uses it only to find the default analysis names. Leave it `NULL` if the object has one receptor table. You must give it if the object has several slots and you use the default names.

`validate`

:   Validate the updated SIRUP object (default `TRUE`)?

## Details

[`dowser::getTrees()`](https://dowser.readthedocs.io/en/latest/topics/getTrees/) takes a tibble of formatted clones and returns a tibble with a `trees` column. `getSpatialTrees` does not change how dowser builds the trees. It reads the formatted clones from the SIRUP object by name (`f_clones_analysis`) and stores the trees in the object as an analysis. The trees and the clone data of each tree then stay with the spatial data. [`plotSpatialCloneTreePairs()`](plotSpatialCloneTreePairs.md) and [`clusterTreesTips()`](clusterTreesTips.md) can use them without more input.

By default, the function builds maximum parsimony trees with `phangorn::pratchet()`. It estimates the branch lengths with `ape::acctran()`. If you use `build = "igphyml"`, the function predicts the values of the internal nodes with maximum parsimony. In this case, give `dir` (a directory for the temporary files) and `id` (a unique name for this analysis). Use a different `id` for each call that shares a `dir`, so that the calls do not overwrite each other\'s files. The function writes `modelfile` if you do not give it. The file has no constraints. The function deletes the temporary files unless you set `rm_temp = FALSE`.

The arguments from `trait` to `...` go to [`dowser::getTrees()`](https://dowser.readthedocs.io/en/latest/topics/getTrees/).

## Value

The updated SIRUP object, with the trees as an analysis.

## See Also

[`formatSpatialClones()`](formatSpatialClones.md), [`clusterTreesTips()`](clusterTreesTips.md), [`plotSpatialCloneTreePairs()`](plotSpatialCloneTreePairs.md)

## Examples

``` R
x <- readSIRUP(system.file("extdata", "sirup_synthetic.rds", package = "SIRUP"))
x <- formatSpatialClones(
  x,
  id = "sequence_id",
  germ = "germline_alignment_d_mask",
  traits = "spatial_id"
)
x <- getSpatialTrees(x)
getAnalysis(x, "trees")
```

functions.title: Install the SIRUP skill for an LLM agent
functions.summary: `installSIRUPSkill` copies the SIRUP skill into the skills folder of an LLM agent.
functions.markdown:
# installSIRUPSkill

## Install the SIRUP skill for an LLM agent

## Description

`installSIRUPSkill` copies the SIRUP skill into the skills folder of an LLM agent. The skill teaches the agent how to use SIRUP: how to build a SIRUP object, which function answers which question, and which checks to run.

## Usage

``` R
installSIRUPSkill(
  agent = c("claude", "codex", "antigravity"),
  install_dir = NULL,
  overwrite = TRUE,
  quiet = FALSE
)
```

## Arguments

`agent`

:   The agent. Use `"claude"` (Claude Code), `"codex"` (Codex), or `"antigravity"` (Antigravity).

`install_dir`

:   The skills folder that receives the skill (default `NULL`). If `NULL`, the function uses the folder of the agent for all your projects. Give a path to install the skill for one project, or to use another folder. The function makes the folder if it does not exist.

`overwrite`

:   Replace a skill that is already in `install_dir` (default `TRUE`)? If `FALSE`, the function stops when the skill exists.

`quiet`

:   Hide the message that says where the skill went (default `FALSE`)?

## Details

A skill is a folder with a file named `SKILL.md`. The file starts with a name and a description. At the start of a session, the agent reads the name and the description of each installed skill. It reads the rest of the folder when your request matches a description.

SIRUP ships its skill in `inst/skills/sirup`. R copies that folder into the SIRUP folder of your R library when it installs the package. An agent does not read your R library. This function copies the skill to the place where the agent looks.

With `install_dir = NULL`, the function uses the skills folder that the agent reads for all your projects:

`agent`
:   Folder for all your projects

`"claude"`
:   `⁠~/.claude/skills⁠`

`"codex"`
:   `⁠~/.agents/skills⁠`

`"antigravity"`
:   `⁠~/.gemini/config/skills⁠`

On Windows, `~` is your user folder (`USERPROFILE`). These folders come from the documentation of each agent. They can change, so check the documentation of your agent if the skill does not appear.

To install the skill for one project only, give the skills folder of the project to `install_dir`. For Claude Code this is `.claude/skills` in the project. For Codex and Antigravity it is `.agents/skills`. A relative path starts in the current working directory.

The function copies the skill to a folder named `sirup` inside `install_dir`. If that folder exists and holds a `SKILL.md` file, the function removes it first, so that no old files stay. If the folder exists but holds no `SKILL.md` file, the function stops. It does not remove a folder that is not a skill.

After the installation, start a new session of the agent and ask which skills it has. Look for `sirup`.

## Value

The path of the installed skill folder, invisibly.

## Examples

``` R
# Install into a temporary folder, so that this example changes nothing on
# your computer. To install for real, leave out `install_dir`.
skills <- file.path(tempdir(), "agent-skills")
installSIRUPSkill("claude", install_dir = skills, quiet = TRUE)
list.files(file.path(skills, "sirup"))

## Not run: 
# Install for all your projects, in the default folder of the agent.
installSIRUPSkill("claude")
installSIRUPSkill("codex")
installSIRUPSkill("antigravity")

# Install for one project only.
installSIRUPSkill("claude", install_dir = ".claude/skills")
installSIRUPSkill("codex", install_dir = ".agents/skills")

## End(Not run)
```

functions.title: Merge SIRUP objects into one multi-sample object
functions.summary: `mergeSIRUP` combines several SIRUP objects into one multi-sample SIRUP object.
functions.markdown:
# mergeSIRUP

## Merge SIRUP objects into one multi-sample object

## Description

`mergeSIRUP` combines several SIRUP objects into one multi-sample SIRUP object.

## Usage

``` R
mergeSIRUP(
  ...,
  samples,
  sample_field = "sample_id",
  keep_analyses = TRUE,
  validate = TRUE
)
```

## Arguments

`...`

:   Two or more SIRUP objects to merge.

`samples`

:   Character vector of sample names. Give one unique, non-empty name for each SIRUP object.

`sample_field`

:   Name of the receptor-table column that holds the sample name (default `"sample_id"`). The function creates the column or checks it.

`keep_analyses`

:   Keep the stored analyses (default `TRUE`)? Each analysis becomes a named list with one entry for each name in `samples`.

`validate`

:   Validate the merged object (default `TRUE`)?

## Details

Each input object becomes one spatial sample, named by `samples`. The function does these steps:

- It sets `sample_field` in each receptor table, then binds the rows. If the objects have several receptor slots, they must have the same slot names. The function binds each slot separately.

- It stores the Seurat objects in a named list.

- It adds the sample name to each stored polygon (if any) and keeps the polygons.

- It stores each analysis as a list with one entry per sample, if `keep_analyses` is `TRUE`.

## Value

A multi-sample SIRUP object.

## See Also

[`createSIRUP()`](createSIRUP.md), [`subsetSIRUP()`](subsetSIRUP.md)

## Examples

``` R
x <- readSIRUP(system.file("extdata", "sirup_synthetic.rds", package = "SIRUP"))
merged <- mergeSIRUP(x, x, samples = c("a", "b"))
spatialSamples(merged)
```

functions.title: Split the rrad tags out of sequence IDs
functions.summary: `parseRadSequenceIds` reads the barcode and the UMI from the sequence IDs of an AIRR table.
functions.markdown:
# parseRadSequenceIds

## Split the rrad tags out of sequence IDs

## Description

`parseRadSequenceIds` reads the barcode and the UMI from the sequence IDs of an AIRR table. It adds them as columns.

## Usage

``` R
parseRadSequenceIds(airr_df, id = "sequence_id", strip = TRUE)
```

## Arguments

`airr_df`

:   AIRR-style data frame.

`id`

:   Name of the column that holds the read IDs (default `"sequence_id"`).

`strip`

:   Replace the ID column with the read ID (default `TRUE`)? The read ID is the part before the first `|` or white space.

## Details

The function reads IDs of the form `id|BARCODE=YYY|UMI=XXX`.

If an ID has no tag, the function keeps the values in an existing `barcode` or `umi` column. A conflict between values, or a repeated tag, gives an error. A missing UMI is allowed. For other header formats, use [`extractSpatialIds()`](extractSpatialIds.md).

The metadata must be in the ID, before any white space, so that it stays in the IgBLAST output. For unformatted rrad output with SAM-style comments, reformat the reads first with `header_format = "presto"`.

## Value

The data frame with the columns `umi` and `barcode` added.

## See Also

[`extractSpatialIds()`](extractSpatialIds.md), [`processSpatialSample()`](processSpatialSample.md)

## Examples

``` R
reads <- data.frame(
  sequence_id = c("read1|BARCODE=ACGTACGT|UMI=TTGCA", "read2|BARCODE=GGGTTTAA|UMI=CCATG")
)
parseRadSequenceIds(reads)
```
