functions.title: Annotate raw reads with IgBLAST
functions.summary: `runIgblast` runs `airrblast::assignGenes()` on raw reads.
functions.markdown:
# runIgblast

## Annotate raw reads with IgBLAST

## Description

`runIgblast` runs `airrblast::assignGenes()` on raw reads. It writes an AIRR table.

## Usage

``` R
runIgblast(
  input,
  output_tsv,
  receptor = c("ig", "tr"),
  organism = "human",
  igblast_base = "~/software/igblast",
  igblast_refs = NULL,
  num_threads = 8
)
```

## Arguments

`input`

:   Path of a FASTA or FASTQ file, optionally gzipped. A plain FASTA file must end in `.fasta` or `.fa`.

`output_tsv`

:   Path of the AIRR TSV file. It must end in `.tsv`.

`receptor`

:   `"ig"` for BCR or `"tr"` for TCR.

`organism`

:   `"human"`, `"mouse"`, or `"rhesus_monkey"`.

`igblast_base`

:   IgBLAST installation folder. It must hold `bin/igblastn`, `internal_data`, and `optional_file`.

`igblast_refs`

:   Folder with the IgBLAST `⁠database/⁠` and `⁠fasta/⁠` folders (the `refs` argument of `airrblast::assignGenes()`). If `NULL`, the function uses `igblast_base`.

`num_threads`

:   Number of threads, passed to `assignGenes()` as `nproc`.

## Details

The input can be FASTA or FASTQ, optionally gzipped. The function first writes gzipped and FASTQ inputs as a plain FASTA next to `output_tsv`. It drops the FASTQ quality strings, because `igblastn` accepts only FASTA. Each call runs one receptor group: `ig` or `tr`.

`assignGenes()` does not search the C-region database, so the tables of raw reads have no `c_call` from this step.

## Value

`output_tsv`, invisibly.

## See Also

[`processSpatialSample()`](processSpatialSample.md), [`parseRadSequenceIds()`](parseRadSequenceIds.md)

## Examples

``` R
## Not run: 
# This example needs IgBLAST and the IgBLAST reference files.
runIgblast(
  "sample1_reads.fasta.gz",
  output_tsv = "sample1_igblast.tsv",
  receptor = "ig",
  organism = "human",
  igblast_base = "~/software/igblast"
)

## End(Not run)
```

functions.title: Select polygon vertices in an interactive app
functions.summary: `selectSpatialPolygons` opens a Shiny app.
functions.markdown:
# selectSpatialPolygons

## Select polygon vertices in an interactive app

## Description

`selectSpatialPolygons` opens a Shiny app. You click polygon vertices on a plot of the spatial coordinates.

## Usage

``` R
selectSpatialPolygons(
  object,
  feature = NULL,
  assay = "Spatial",
  layer = "counts",
  images = NULL,
  image_scale = NULL,
  swap_coords = NULL,
  save_path = NULL,
  plot_image = FALSE,
  downsample_n = NULL,
  downsample_seed = 1L,
  point_size = 0.8,
  point_alpha = 0.9,
  show_zeros = TRUE,
  launch_browser = TRUE,
  host = getOption("shiny.host", "127.0.0.1"),
  port = getOption("shiny.port", NULL),
  quiet = TRUE
)
```

## Arguments

`object`

:   Seurat object or SIRUP object.

`feature`

:   Feature to show as a color scale under the vertices. You can change it in the app. The function looks in the assay first. If the feature is not there, it looks in the object metadata. This lets you show module scores (from `AddModuleScore()`, `UCell`, or any numeric column) without adding them to an assay.

`assay`

:   Assay to set before the function gets the feature values (default `"Spatial"`).

`layer`

:   Expression layer to use for `feature` (default `"counts"`).

`images`

:   Names of the Seurat images to use.

`image_scale`

:   Image scale for `SeuratObject::GetTissueCoordinates()`. If `NULL`, the function uses the value stored in the SIRUP object.

`swap_coords`

:   Swap the two Seurat coordinate axes? If `NULL`, the function uses the value stored in the SIRUP object. Give a value if `object` is a Seurat object.

`save_path`

:   Path of a CSV file to save the vertices to.

`plot_image`

:   Show the Seurat tissue image under the points (default `FALSE`)?

`downsample_n`

:   Number of points to show in the app. If `NULL`, the app shows all points. A click still snaps to the nearest spatial ID in the full coordinate table.

`downsample_seed`

:   Random seed for the downsampling (default 1).

`point_size`

:   Size of the points (default 0.8).

`point_alpha`

:   Starting opacity of the points (default 0.9).

`show_zeros`

:   Show the points where `feature` is zero or `NA` (default `TRUE`)? On sparse Visium HD data, the zeros can hide the signal. Use `FALSE`, or clear \"Show zero points\" in the app, to show only the positive points. This changes the display only. A click can still select a hidden point as a vertex.

`launch_browser`

:   Passed to `shiny::runApp()` (default `TRUE`).

`host`

:   Host for `shiny::runApp()`. Set it when you run the function in an interactive HPC session through an SSH tunnel.

`port`

:   Port for `shiny::runApp()`. Set it when you run the function in an interactive HPC session through an SSH tunnel.

`quiet`

:   Hide warnings while the app runs (default `TRUE`)?

## Details

Each click snaps to the nearest spatial ID. Click \"Close polygon\" or \"New polygon\" before you finish. This repeats the first vertex at the end of each polygon.

The vertices can describe overlapping or nested polygons. The function that receives the vertices decides the membership: [`assignSpatialPolygons()`](assignSpatialPolygons.md), [`assignReceptorPolygons()`](assignReceptorPolygons.md), [`createSIRUP()`](createSIRUP.md), or [`addPolygons()`](sirup-polygons.md). The primary `polygon_id` gets the ID of the smallest matching polygon by area. The logical `⁠polygon_<ID>⁠` columns show membership in each polygon.

## Value

A data frame with the columns `spatial_id`, `x`, `y`, `num`, `polygon`, and `image`.

## See Also

[`formatSpatialPolygons()`](formatSpatialPolygons.md), [`addPolygons()`](sirup-polygons.md), [`plotSpatialPolygons()`](plotSpatialPolygons.md)

## Examples

``` R

x <- readSIRUP(system.file("extdata", "sirup_synthetic.rds", package = "SIRUP"))

# Click the vertices in the app. Use "Close polygon" when you finish.
polygons <- selectSpatialPolygons(
  getSpatial(x),
  image_scale = "hires",
  swap_coords = FALSE
)
```

functions.title: Subset a Seurat object to the spots inside polygons
functions.summary: `seuratSubsetPolygon` keeps only the spatial IDs inside the polygons.
functions.markdown:
# seuratSubsetPolygon

## Subset a Seurat object to the spots inside polygons

## Description

`seuratSubsetPolygon` keeps only the spatial IDs inside the polygons. It also records the polygon of each spot in the metadata.

## Usage

``` R
seuratSubsetPolygon(
  object,
  polygon = NULL,
  images = NULL,
  image_scale = NULL,
  swap_coords = NULL,
  polygon_val = NULL,
  x = "x",
  y = "y",
  polygon_id = "polygon",
  metadata = "polygon",
  include_boundary = TRUE
)
```

## Arguments

`object`

:   Seurat object, or a named list of Seurat objects.

`polygon`

:   Data frame of polygon vertices in order. It needs the columns set by `x` and `y`. If the column set by `polygon_id` exists, the function treats each polygon on its own.

`images`

:   Names of the Seurat images to use.

`image_scale`

:   Image scale for `SeuratObject::GetTissueCoordinates()`.

`swap_coords`

:   Swap the two Seurat coordinate axes? You must give a value.

`polygon_val`

:   IDs of the polygons to use. If `NULL`, the function uses all polygons.

`x`

:   Name of the x-coordinate column in `polygon` (default `"x"`).

`y`

:   Name of the y-coordinate column in `polygon` (default `"y"`).

`polygon_id`

:   Name of the column in `polygon` that groups the vertices by polygon (default `"polygon"`).

`metadata`

:   Name of the metadata column that holds the primary polygon of each spot (default `"polygon"`). A spot in overlapping polygons gets the smallest polygon by area.

`include_boundary`

:   Count spots on a polygon edge as inside the polygon (default `TRUE`)?

## Value

A Seurat object with only the spatial IDs inside the selected polygons. For a list of Seurat objects, a list of the subset objects. The function drops an object with no spot inside a polygon. It adds the `metadata` column to `⁠@meta.data⁠`.

## See Also

[`assignSpatialPolygons()`](assignSpatialPolygons.md)

## Examples

``` R
x <- readSIRUP(system.file("extdata", "sirup_synthetic.rds", package = "SIRUP"))
flat <- data.frame(
  polygon = "block",
  x = c(3.5, 5.5, 5.5, 3.5),
  y = c(0.5, 0.5, 2.5, 2.5)
)

# Keep the four spots inside the polygon.
subset <- seuratSubsetPolygon(
  getSpatial(x),
  polygon = flat,
  image_scale = "hires",
  swap_coords = FALSE
)
ncol(subset)
```

functions.summary: `getSpatial` returns the Seurat object(s).
functions.markdown:
# sirup-accessors

## Extract data from a SIRUP object

## Description

`getSpatial` returns the Seurat object(s). `spatialSamples` returns the spatial sample names. `getReceptors` returns one receptor table. `receptorSlots` returns the names of the receptor slots.

## Usage

``` R
getSpatial(x, sample_id = NULL)

spatialSamples(x)

getReceptors(x, sample_id = NULL, slot = NULL)

receptorSlots(x)
```

## Arguments

`x`

:   A SIRUP object.

`sample_id`

:   Name of one spatial sample. Use it only if the object holds a named list of Seurat objects.

`slot`

:   Name of the receptor slot. If the object has one receptor table, leave it `NULL` (the slot is called `"only_slot"`). If the object has several slots, you must give one.

## Value

`getSpatial` returns the Seurat object. For a multi-sample object, it returns the named list of Seurat objects, or one Seurat object if you give `sample_id`. `spatialSamples` returns a character vector of sample names. `getReceptors` returns the receptor tibble of one slot. If you give `sample_id`, it returns only the rows for that sample. `receptorSlots` returns a character vector of slot names.

## See Also

[`getPolygons()`](sirup-polygons.md), [`getAnalysis()`](sirup-analyses.md)

## Examples

``` R
x <- readSIRUP(system.file("extdata", "sirup_synthetic.rds", package = "SIRUP"))
getSpatial(x)
head(getReceptors(x))
spatialSamples(x)
receptorSlots(x)
```

functions.title: Store and retrieve analyses in a SIRUP object
functions.summary: `getAnalysis` returns one stored result.
functions.markdown:
# sirup-analyses

## Store and retrieve analyses in a SIRUP object

## Description

`getAnalysis` returns one stored result. `setAnalysis` adds or replaces a result. `listAnalyses` returns the names of the stored results. `removeAnalysis` deletes a result.

## Usage

``` R
getAnalysis(x, name, sample_id = NULL)

setAnalysis(x, name, value, sample_id = NULL, validate = TRUE)

listAnalyses(x)

removeAnalysis(x, name, validate = TRUE)
```

## Arguments

`x`

: A SIRUP object.

`name`

: Name of the analysis. Give one non-empty character string.

`sample_id`

: Name of a spatial sample. Use it to store or get a result for one sample.

`value`

: R object to store. It can be `NULL`.

`validate`

: Validate the updated SIRUP object?

## Details

The `analyses` list of a SIRUP object holds any R object. Use it to keep derived results with the data that produced them. Examples are Dowser clones and trees, spatial statistics, and polygon summaries.

## Value

`getAnalysis` returns the stored object. `listAnalyses` returns a character vector. `setAnalysis` and `removeAnalysis` return the updated SIRUP object.

## See Also

[`updateAnalysis()`](sirup-transform.md), [`mergeSIRUP()`](mergeSIRUP.md)

## Examples

``` R
x <- readSIRUP(system.file("extdata", "sirup_synthetic.rds", package = "SIRUP"))
x <- setAnalysis(x, "n_clones", 5)
listAnalyses(x)
getAnalysis(x, "n_clones")
x <- removeAnalysis(x, "n_clones")
listAnalyses(x)
```

functions.title: Save and read SIRUP objects
functions.summary: `saveSIRUP` writes a SIRUP object to one RDS file.
functions.markdown:
# sirup-io

## Save and read SIRUP objects

## Description

`saveSIRUP` writes a SIRUP object to one RDS file. `readSIRUP` reads the file back.

## Usage

``` R
saveSIRUP(x, file, ...)

readSIRUP(file)
```

## Arguments

`x`

:   A SIRUP object from [`createSIRUP()`](createSIRUP.md).

`file`

:   Path of the RDS file. A `.sirup.rds` extension is a good choice, but any path works.

`...`

:   Other arguments for [`saveRDS()`](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/base/html/readRDS.html), for example `compress`.

## Details

`saveSIRUP` validates the object. It stores the versions of SIRUP and SeuratObject that write the file.

`readSIRUP` does these steps:

1.  It converts an object that was saved under the old package name, SIRAP (class `sirap`), to the current names.

2.  It upgrades an older object to the current schema.

3.  It gives a warning if the versions of SIRUP or SeuratObject that wrote the file differ from the installed versions.

4.  It validates the object, then returns it.

## Value

`saveSIRUP` returns `file`, invisibly. `readSIRUP` returns the validated SIRUP object.

## See Also

[`createSIRUP()`](createSIRUP.md), [`validateSIRUP()`](validateSIRUP.md)

## Examples

``` R
x <- readSIRUP(system.file("extdata", "sirup_synthetic.rds", package = "SIRUP"))

# Save the object to a temporary file, then read it back.
path <- saveSIRUP(x, tempfile(fileext = ".sirup.rds"))
x2 <- readSIRUP(path)
x2
```

functions.title: Add or retrieve polygon geometry from a SIRUP object
functions.summary: `addPolygons` stores a polygon table in a SIRUP object.
functions.markdown:
# sirup-polygons

## Add or retrieve polygon geometry from a SIRUP object

## Description

`addPolygons` stores a polygon table in a SIRUP object. It replaces any stored polygons. `getPolygons` returns the stored table.

## Usage

``` R
getPolygons(x, sample_id = NULL)

addPolygons(
  x,
  polygons = NULL,
  polygons_path = NULL,
  sample_id = NULL,
  include_boundary = TRUE,
  validate = TRUE
)
```

## Arguments

`x`

: A SIRUP object.

`sample_id`

: Sample name or names to add to the polygons from `polygons_path`. Use it only if the paths have no names.

`polygons`

: Polygon table.

`polygons_path`

: Path to a flat CSV file of polygon vertices. For a multi-sample object, give a named vector or list of paths, with one path for each sample.

`include_boundary`

: Count spots on a polygon edge as members of the polygon?

`validate`

: Validate the updated object?

## Details

The input to `addPolygons` can be a nested tibble with `polygon_id` and `vertices` columns. It can also be a flat vertex table, such as the CSV file from [`selectSpatialPolygons()`](selectSpatialPolygons.md).

The function adds a `polygon_id` column to both the Seurat metadata and the receptor table. If a barcode lies in overlapping or nested polygons, it gets the ID of the smallest polygon by area. The function also adds one logical `⁠polygon_<ID>⁠` column for each polygon. These columns show membership in every polygon as booleans.

## Value

`getPolygons` returns a polygon tibble. `addPolygons` returns the updated SIRUP object.

## See Also

[`selectSpatialPolygons()`](selectSpatialPolygons.md), [`createSIRUP()`](createSIRUP.md)

## Examples

``` R
x <- readSIRUP(system.file("extdata", "sirup_synthetic.rds", package = "SIRUP"))
getPolygons(x)

# Replace the stored polygons with one polygon in the middle of the data.
center <- tibble::tibble(
  polygon_id = "center",
  vertices = list(data.frame(x = c(2.5, 3.5, 3.5, 2.5), y = c(2.5, 2.5, 3.5, 3.5)))
)
x2 <- addPolygons(x, center)
getPolygons(x2)$polygon_id
```

functions.title: Update data stored in a SIRUP object
functions.summary: `updateReceptors`, `updateSpatial`, and `updateAnalysis` apply a function to one part of a SIRUP object.
functions.markdown:
# sirup-transform

## Update data stored in a SIRUP object

## Description

`updateReceptors`, `updateSpatial`, and `updateAnalysis` apply a function to one part of a SIRUP object. They return the updated SIRUP object.

## Usage

``` R
updateReceptors(
  x,
  fun,
  ...,
  sample_id = NULL,
  slot = NULL,
  receptor_fields = NULL,
  validate = TRUE
)

updateSpatial(x, fun, ..., sample_id = NULL, validate = TRUE)

updateAnalysis(x, name, fun, ..., sample_id = NULL, validate = TRUE)
```

## Arguments

`x`

:   A SIRUP object.

`fun`

:   Function, or the name of a function. The function receives the selected part of the SIRUP object as its first argument.

`...`

:   Other arguments for `fun`.

`sample_id`

:   Name of the spatial sample to update. Use it only for multi-sample objects.

`slot`

:   Name of the receptor slot that `updateReceptors` changes. Leave it `NULL` if the object has one receptor table. You must give it if the object has several slots.

`receptor_fields`

:   Named list of receptor field mappings to change. The names can be `spatial_id`, `image`, `sample`, `clone`, `locus`, or `count`. A `NULL` value clears an optional mapping.

`validate`

:   Validate the updated SIRUP object?

`name`

:   Name of the stored analysis. Give one non-empty character string.

## Details

`updateReceptors` needs a function that returns a data frame. The function stores the result as a tibble and keeps the existing field mappings. If the object has no clone field and the result has a `clone_id` column, the function records `clone_id` as the clone field. Use `receptor_fields` to set or clear a mapping yourself. If you give `sample_id`, the function applies `fun` to the rows of that sample only. It then puts the result back in the full table. If the object has several receptor slots, `slot` chooses the table that `fun` changes. The other slots stay as they are. The field mappings are shared by all slots. The `spatial_id` and `sample` columns must stay in every slot. The other mapped columns, such as `clone_id`, must stay in at least one slot.

`updateSpatial` needs a function that returns a Seurat object. In a multi-sample object, it applies `fun` to every Seurat object. If you give `sample_id`, it updates only that object.

`updateAnalysis` applies `fun` to the stored result called `name`. To store a new result, use [`setAnalysis()`](sirup-analyses.md).

## Value

The updated SIRUP object.

## See Also

[`getReceptors()`](sirup-accessors.md), [`getSpatial()`](sirup-accessors.md), [`setAnalysis()`](sirup-analyses.md)

## Examples

``` R
x <- readSIRUP(system.file("extdata", "sirup_synthetic.rds", package = "SIRUP"))

# Remove the sequences in clone 3.
x2 <- updateReceptors(x, dplyr::filter, clone_id != "3")
nrow(getReceptors(x2))

# Add a Seurat metadata column.
x3 <- updateSpatial(x, function(spatial) {
  spatial$gene_rich <- spatial$nFeature_Spatial >= 8
  spatial
})
table(getSpatial(x3)$gene_rich)

# Change a stored result.
x4 <- setAnalysis(x, "n_clones", 5)
x4 <- updateAnalysis(x4, "n_clones", function(value) value + 1)
getAnalysis(x4, "n_clones")
```

functions.title: Calculate clonal dominance inside polygons
functions.summary: `spatialCloneDominance` calculates the share of each clone among the receptors inside spatial polygons.
functions.markdown:
# spatialCloneDominance

## Calculate clonal dominance inside polygons

## Description

`spatialCloneDominance` calculates the share of each clone among the receptors inside spatial polygons.

## Usage

``` R
spatialCloneDominance(
  receptors = NULL,
  object = NULL,
  polygon = NULL,
  spatial_id = NULL,
  clone = "clone_id",
  locus_val = NULL,
  locus = "locus",
  count = NULL,
  v_call = "v_call",
  exclude_singletons = FALSE,
  images = NULL,
  image_scale = NULL,
  swap_coords = NULL,
  polygon_val = NULL,
  x = "x",
  y = "y",
  polygon_id = "polygon",
  include_boundary = TRUE,
  slot = NULL
)
```

## Arguments

`receptors`

:   AIRR-style receptor table with clone IDs and a spatial ID column. You can give a SIRUP object here if you omit `object`.

`object`

:   Seurat object or SIRUP object. If it is a SIRUP object, you can omit `receptors`.

`polygon`

:   Data frame of polygon vertices in order. It needs the columns set by `x` and `y`. If the column set by `polygon_id` exists, the function treats each polygon on its own. If `object` is a SIRUP object and `polygon` is `NULL`, the function uses the stored polygons.

`spatial_id`

:   Name of the `receptors` column that holds the spatial IDs. If `NULL`, the function uses the stored field of a SIRUP object, or looks for a standard spatial ID column.

`clone`

:   Name of the `receptors` column that holds the clone IDs (default `"clone_id"`).

`locus_val`

:   Locus values to keep, for example `"IGH"`. If `NULL`, the function keeps all loci.

`locus`

:   Name of the `receptors` column that holds the locus (default `"locus"`).

`count`

:   Name of the numeric `receptors` column that holds the counts. If `NULL`, each receptor row counts as one.

`v_call`

:   Name of the `receptors` column that holds the V-gene calls (default `"v_call"`). If the column exists, the function also returns the V genes of each clone at three levels: with allele, without allele, and V-gene superfamily.

`exclude_singletons`

:   Exclude clones that have only one receptor row after the locus filter (default `FALSE`)?

`images`

:   Names of the Seurat images to use.

`image_scale`

:   Image scale for `SeuratObject::GetTissueCoordinates()`. If `NULL`, the function uses the value stored in the SIRUP object.

`swap_coords`

:   Swap the two Seurat coordinate axes? If `NULL`, the function uses the value stored in the SIRUP object. Give a value if `object` is a Seurat object.

`polygon_val`

:   IDs of the polygons to use. If `NULL`, the function uses all polygons.

`x`

:   Name of the x-coordinate column in `polygon` (default `"x"`).

`y`

:   Name of the y-coordinate column in `polygon` (default `"y"`).

`polygon_id`

:   Name of the column in `polygon` that groups the vertices by polygon (default `"polygon"`).

`include_boundary`

:   Count spots on a polygon edge as inside the polygon (default `TRUE`)? The function ignores this argument if `object` is a SIRUP object with stored polygon annotations and `polygon` is `NULL`.

`slot`

:   Name of the receptor slot to use. Leave it `NULL` if the SIRUP object has one receptor table. You must give it if the object has several slots. The function ignores `slot` if you give a plain receptor table.

## Details

The function finds the spatial IDs whose coordinates lie inside each polygon. It keeps the receptor rows with those spatial IDs. Then it calculates the fraction of these receptors that belong to each clone.

If you give a SIRUP object and omit `clone`, `locus`, or `count`, the function uses the field names stored in the object. If you omit `polygon`, it uses the stored polygons.

## Value

An object of class `sirup_spatial_clone_dominance`. It is a list with these items: `dominance` (the dominance table), `region_spatial_ids`, `region_coordinates`, `region_receptors`, `polygons` (the vertices prepared for plotting), and `metadata` (the receptor field names that the function used).

## See Also

[`plotSpatialRegionReceptors()`](plotSpatialRegionReceptors.md), [`plotSpatialPolygonPies()`](plotSpatialPolygonPies.md), [`plotSpatialCloneDensity3D()`](plotSpatialCloneDensity3D.md)

## Examples

``` R
x <- readSIRUP(system.file("extdata", "sirup_synthetic.rds", package = "SIRUP"))

# Use the polygons stored in the SIRUP object.
dominance <- spatialCloneDominance(x)
dominance$dominance[, c("polygon_id", "clone_id", "n_receptors", "proportion")]
```

functions.title: Test clone localization with join counts
functions.summary: `spatialCloneJoinCount` tests if each clone clusters in space.
functions.markdown:
# spatialCloneJoinCount

## Test clone localization with join counts

## Description

`spatialCloneJoinCount` tests if each clone clusters in space.

## Usage

``` R
spatialCloneJoinCount(
  object,
  receptors = NULL,
  clone = NULL,
  spatial_id = NULL,
  clone_val = NULL,
  polygon = NULL,
  polygon_val = NULL,
  images = NULL,
  image_scale = NULL,
  swap_coords = NULL,
  x = "x",
  y = "y",
  polygon_id = "polygon",
  include_boundary = TRUE,
  min_spatial_ids = 2,
  radius = NULL,
  k = 6,
  alternative = "greater",
  other_label = "Other",
  use_stored_polygons = NULL,
  return_data = FALSE,
  slot = NULL
)
```

## Arguments

`object`

:   Seurat object or SIRUP object.

`receptors`

:   AIRR-style receptor table with spatial IDs and clone IDs. Omit if `object` is a SIRUP object.

`clone`

:   Name of the `receptors` column that holds the clone IDs. If `object` is a SIRUP object and this argument is `NULL`, the function uses the stored clone field, if there is one.

`spatial_id`

:   Name of the `receptors` column that holds the spatial IDs. If `object` is a SIRUP object and this argument is `NULL`, the function uses the stored spatial ID field. Give a value if you use separate Seurat and receptor objects.

`clone_val`

:   Clone IDs to test. If `NULL`, the function tests all clones that occur in at least `min_spatial_ids` spatial IDs.

`polygon`

:   Data frame of polygon vertices. The function tests only the spots inside these polygons (default `NULL`).

`polygon_val`

:   Polygon IDs to select from `polygon`.

`images`

:   Names of the Seurat images to use.

`image_scale`

:   Image scale for `SeuratObject::GetTissueCoordinates()`. If `NULL`, the function uses the value stored in the SIRUP object.

`swap_coords`

:   Swap the two Seurat coordinate axes? If `NULL`, the function uses the value stored in the SIRUP object. Give a value if `object` is a Seurat object.

`x`

:   Name of the x-coordinate column in `polygon` (default `"x"`).

`y`

:   Name of the y-coordinate column in `polygon` (default `"y"`).

`polygon_id`

:   Name of the column in `polygon` that groups the vertices by polygon (default `"polygon"`).

`include_boundary`

:   Count spots on a polygon edge as inside the polygon (default `TRUE`)? The function ignores this argument if `object` is a SIRUP object with stored polygons and `polygon` is `NULL`. In that case, it uses the stored polygon annotations.

`min_spatial_ids`

:   Smallest number of spatial IDs that a clone needs to be tested (default 2).

`radius`

:   Distance that defines a neighborhood. If `NULL`, the function uses `k`.

`k`

:   Number of nearest neighbors, used if `radius` is `NULL` (default 6).

`alternative`

:   Alternative hypothesis for `spdep::joincount.test()` (default `"greater"`).

`other_label`

:   Label for the spatial IDs that do not contain the tested clone (default `"Other"`).

`use_stored_polygons`

:   Run one test for each stored polygon of a SIRUP object? Use `TRUE` to require stored polygons. Use `FALSE` to build one neighbor graph for each sample and ignore stored polygons. If `NULL` (default), the function uses `TRUE` when a SIRUP object has stored polygons and you give no `polygon`. Otherwise, it uses `FALSE`.

`return_data`

:   Return the data used for each test (default `FALSE`)?

`slot`

:   Name of the receptor slot to use. Leave it `NULL` if the SIRUP object has one receptor table. You must give it if the object has several slots and the function reads receptors. The function ignores `slot` if you give a plain receptor table.

## Details

The function calls `spdep::joincount.test()` for each clone. The test asks if neighboring spots with receptors share the clone more often than random labels would give.

The function skips a clone if it occurs in fewer than `min_spatial_ids` spatial IDs, or in every spatial ID of the region.

If `object` is a SIRUP object with stored polygons and you give no `polygon`, the function runs one test for each stored polygon. Set `use_stored_polygons` to FALSE to change this.

If the data come from more than one image, or a sirup object with multiple samples, then the function builds one graph and runs one test for each sample or image.

## Value

A list with these items: `summary` (a table with one row for each tested clone and region, ordered by p-value), `tests` (the `spdep` test results), `data` (the data for each test, or `NULL` if `return_data` is `FALSE`), `neighbors`, `weights`, `radius`, `k`, `alternative`, and `min_spatial_ids`.

## See Also

[`plotSpatialCloneJoinCount()`](plotSpatialCloneJoinCount.md), [`spatialMoran()`](spatialMoran.md)

## Examples

``` R
x <- readSIRUP(system.file("extdata", "sirup_synthetic.rds", package = "SIRUP"))

# Test each clone on the whole tissue.
join_count <- spatialCloneJoinCount(
  x,
  use_stored_polygons = FALSE,
  k = 4,
  return_data = TRUE
)
join_count$summary[, c("clone_id", "observed_join_count", "expected_join_count", "p_value")]
```

functions.title: Summarize the spatial spread of clones
functions.summary: `spatialCloneSpread` gives the distances between the spots of each clone in each sample.
functions.markdown:
# spatialCloneSpread

## Summarize the spatial spread of clones

## Description

`spatialCloneSpread` gives the distances between the spots of each clone in each sample.

## Usage

``` R
spatialCloneSpread(
  object,
  receptors = NULL,
  clone = NULL,
  spatial_id = NULL,
  clone_val = NULL,
  images = NULL,
  image_scale = NULL,
  swap_coords = NULL,
  min_spatial_ids = 2L,
  collapse_within_spot = FALSE,
  slot = NULL
)
```

## Arguments

`object`

:   SIRUP object, or Seurat object with spatial images. For a Seurat object, give `receptors`.

`receptors`

:   AIRR-style receptor table. Omit it if `object` is a SIRUP object.

`clone`

:   Name of the column that holds the clone IDs. If `NULL`, the function uses the stored clone field of a SIRUP object, if there is one.

`spatial_id`

:   Name of the column that holds the spatial IDs. If `NULL`, the function uses the stored spatial ID field of a SIRUP object.

`clone_val`

:   Clone IDs to keep.

`images`

:   Names of the images or samples to include.

`image_scale`

:   Image scale for the Seurat image coordinates.

`swap_coords`

:   Swap the x and y coordinates before the function calculates distances?

`min_spatial_ids`

:   Smallest number of observations that a clone needs in a sample (default 2). If `collapse_within_spot` is `TRUE`, the function counts distinct spots. Otherwise, it counts sequences.

`collapse_within_spot`

:   Merge the sequences that share a spatial ID into one point before the function calculates distances (default `FALSE`)? If `FALSE`, the function counts every sequence, so sequences in the same spot give pairs with distance zero. Use `TRUE` to measure the spread over distinct spots only.

`slot`

:   Name of the receptor slot to use. Leave it `NULL` if the SIRUP object has one receptor table. You must give it if the object has several slots and the function reads receptors. The function ignores `slot` if you give a plain receptor table.

## Details

For each sample and clone, the function calculates the distance between every pair of points. It reports the mean and the maximum distance.

## Value

A tibble with one row for each sample and clone. The columns are `sample`, `clone_id`, `n_spatial_ids`, `mean_pairwise_distance`, and `max_pairwise_distance`.

## See Also

[`spatialCloneJoinCount()`](spatialCloneJoinCount.md)

## Examples

``` R
x <- readSIRUP(system.file("extdata", "sirup_synthetic.rds", package = "SIRUP"))
spatialCloneSpread(x)
```

functions.markdown:
# spatialCloneTreePairsToPDF

## Save the tree and map pairs to a PDF file

## Description

`spatialCloneTreePairsToPDF` writes one page for each clone to a PDF file. Each page shows the tree and the tissue map of the clone side by side.

## Usage

``` R
spatialCloneTreePairsToPDF(
  pairs,
  path,
  width = 12,
  height = 6,
  rel_widths = c(1.2, 1),
  nproc = 1L
)
```

## Arguments

`pairs`

:   Result of [`plotSpatialCloneTreePairs()`](plotSpatialCloneTreePairs.md).

`path`

:   Path of the PDF file.

`width`

:   Width of a page, in inches (default 12).

`height`

:   Height of a page, in inches (default 6).

`rel_widths`

:   Relative widths of the tree panel and the map panel (default `c(1.2, 1)`).

`nproc`

:   Number of processes for the pages (default 1). The function needs the `qpdf` package to join the pages that it makes in parallel. If `qpdf` is not installed, it makes the pages one after the other.

## Value

`path`, invisibly.

## See Also

[`plotSpatialCloneTreePairs()`](plotSpatialCloneTreePairs.md)

## Examples

``` R
x <- readSIRUP(system.file("extdata", "sirup_synthetic.rds", package = "SIRUP"))
x <- formatSpatialClones(
  x,
  id = "sequence_id",
  germ = "germline_alignment_d_mask",
  traits = "spatial_id"
)
x <- getSpatialTrees(x)
trees <- getAnalysis(x, "trees")

pairs <- plotSpatialCloneTreePairs(trees, x, clone_val = c("1", "4"))
spatialCloneTreePairsToPDF(pairs, tempfile(fileext = ".pdf"))
```

# spatialDiscretePlot

## Plot a metadata column on a tissue image

## Description

`spatialDiscretePlot` colors each spot by the value of a metadata column. It leaves out the spots that have the \"zero_value\" value.

## Usage

``` R
spatialDiscretePlot(
  object,
  meta_col,
  zero_value = 0,
  images = NULL,
  sample_id = NULL,
  image_scale = NULL,
  swap_coords = NULL,
  cols = NULL,
  point_size = 1.6,
  point_alpha = 1,
  order_points = TRUE,
  image_alpha = 1,
  zoom = FALSE,
  combine = TRUE,
  combine_sample_plots = FALSE
)
```

## Arguments

`object`

:   Seurat object or SIRUP object.

`meta_col`

:   Name of the metadata column to plot.

`zero_value`

:   Value that means \"not present\" (default 0). The function does not draw these spots.

`images`

:   Names of the Seurat images to use.

`sample_id`

:   Names of the samples to plot. Use it for multi-sample SIRUP objects. If `NULL`, the function plots all samples.

`image_scale`

:   Image scale for `SeuratObject::GetTissueCoordinates()`. If `NULL`, the function uses the value stored in the SIRUP object.

`swap_coords`

:   Swap the two Seurat coordinate axes? If `NULL`, the function uses the value stored in the SIRUP object. Give a value if `object` is a Seurat object.

`cols`

:   Named vector of colors, one for each value.

`point_size`

:   Size of the spots. The default is 1.6.

`point_alpha`

:   Opacity of the spots.

`order_points`

:   Draw the low numeric values, or the early factor levels, first, so that the high or late values show on top (default `TRUE`)?

`image_alpha`

:   Opacity of the tissue image.

`zoom`

:   Zoom to the plotted spots (default `FALSE`)? If `FALSE`, the plot shows the full tissue area that the spatial coordinates cover.

`combine`

:   Combine the panels with patchwork, if possible (default `TRUE`)?

`combine_sample_plots`

:   Combine the plots of all samples into one patchwork (default `FALSE`)? The function uses it only for multi-sample objects. If `FALSE`, it returns a named list with one plot for each sample.

## Details

#\' If the object has multiple images or samples, the function draws one plot for each image or sample.

## Value

A ggplot object, a patchwork object, or a list of plots. The function returns `NULL` if all spots have the blank value.

## See Also

[`spatialExpressionPlot()`](spatialExpressionPlot.md)

## Examples

``` R

```

functions.title: Calculate global Lee's L
functions.summary: `spatialLee` tests the spatial association between two continuous variables.
functions.markdown:
# spatialLee

## Calculate global Lee\'s L

## Description

`spatialLee` tests the spatial association between two continuous variables.

## Usage

``` R
spatialLee(
  object,
  x,
  y,
  x_type = c("feature", "metadata"),
  y_type = c("feature", "metadata"),
  assay = NULL,
  layer = "counts",
  images = NULL,
  image_scale = NULL,
  swap_coords = NULL,
  radius = NULL,
  k = 6,
  alternative = "greater",
  method = c("analytical", "mc"),
  nsim = 999,
  progress = FALSE
)
```

## Arguments

`object`

:   Seurat object or SIRUP object.

`x`

:   Name of the first variable. It is a feature or a numeric metadata column.

`y`

:   Name of the second variable. It is a feature or a numeric metadata column.

`x_type`

:   Type of `x`: `feature` or `metadata`.

`y_type`

:   Type of `y`: `feature` or `metadata`.

`assay`

:   Assay to use if `x_type` or `y_type` is `"feature"`.

`layer`

:   Seurat expression layer to use for features (default `"counts"`).

`images`

:   Names of the Seurat images to use.

`image_scale`

:   Image scale for `SeuratObject::GetTissueCoordinates()`. If `NULL`, the function uses the value stored in the SIRUP object.

`swap_coords`

:   Swap the two Seurat coordinate axes? If `NULL`, the function uses the value stored in the SIRUP object. Give a value if `object` is a Seurat object.

`radius`

:   Distance that defines a neighborhood. If `NULL`, the function uses `k`.

`k`

:   Number of nearest neighbors, used if `radius` is `NULL` (default 6). Use `k = 8` for Visium HD, where the bins form a square grid. Use `k = 6` for standard Visium, where the spots form a hexagonal grid.

`alternative`

:   Alternative hypothesis for the significance test (default `"greater"`).

`method`

:   Significance test: `analytical` or `mc` (permutation). See Details.

`nsim`

:   Number of permutations for `method = "mc"` (default 999).

`progress`

:   Show a progress bar for the permutations (default `FALSE`)? The function uses it only if `method = "mc"`. Each permutation re-lags both variables over every spot. For Visium HD, a large `nsim` takes minutes for each pair.

## Details

The function builds one neighbor graph from all spots, with `radius` or `k` as in [`spatialMoran()`](spatialMoran.md). For example, give two gene names to test if the expression of one gene relates to the expression of the second gene in neighboring spots.

`method = "analytical"` calls `spdep::lee.test()`. This function builds a dense n by n weights matrix. The memory use grows with the square of the number of spots, so be careful with larger datasets, like with Visium HD. For large datasets, use `method = "mc"`. It calls `spdep::lee.mc()`, which permutes the labels. It keeps the weights sparse and needs only a few GB.

If the data come from more than one image, or a sirup object with multiple samples, then the function builds one graph and runs one test for each sample or image.

## Value

A list with these items: `test` (the test result), `L` (the observed Lee\'s L), `method`, `data` (the values tested), `neighbors` and `weights` (from `spdep`), `radius`, `k`, `x`, `y`, `x_type`, and `y_type`.

## See Also

[`spatialMoran()`](spatialMoran.md), [`spatialLocalMoran()`](spatialLocalMoran.md)

## Examples

``` R
x <- readSIRUP(system.file("extdata", "sirup_synthetic.rds", package = "SIRUP"))

# Test if gene1 and gene2 are associated.
spatialLee(x, "gene1", "gene2", k = 4)$L

# Use permutations. This method also works for large Visium HD data.
set.seed(1)
spatialLee(x, "gene1", "gene2", k = 4, method = "mc", nsim = 99)$test
```

functions.title: Calculate local Moran's I (LISA)
functions.summary: `spatialLocalMoran` calculates local Moran\'s I for each spot.
functions.markdown:
# spatialLocalMoran

## Calculate local Moran\'s I (LISA)

## Description

`spatialLocalMoran` calculates local Moran\'s I for each spot. It shows where high or low values cluster.

## Usage

``` R
spatialLocalMoran(
  object,
  variable,
  variable_type = c("feature", "metadata", "receptor", "clone"),
  value = NULL,
  receptors = NULL,
  spatial_id = NULL,
  clone = NULL,
  assay = NULL,
  layer = "counts",
  images = NULL,
  image_scale = NULL,
  swap_coords = NULL,
  radius = NULL,
  k = 6,
  slot = NULL
)
```

## Arguments

`object`

:   Seurat object or SIRUP object.

`variable`

:   Name of the feature or the metadata column to test.

`variable_type`

:   Type of `variable`: `feature` (gene expression), `metadata` (Seurat metadata column), `receptor` (receptor table column), or `clone` (clone ID).

`value`

:   Metadata value to convert to a 0/1 indicator (default `NULL`).

`receptors`

:   AIRR-style receptor table. You must give it if `variable_type` is `"receptor"` or `"clone"` and `object` is not a SIRUP object.

`spatial_id`

:   Name of the `receptors` column that holds the spatial IDs. If `object` is a SIRUP object and this argument is `NULL`, the function uses the stored spatial ID field. Give a value if you use separate Seurat and receptor objects.

`clone`

:   Name of the `receptors` column that holds the clone IDs. The function uses it only if `variable_type` is `"clone"`. If `object` is a SIRUP object and this argument is `NULL`, the function uses the stored clone field, if there is one.

`assay`

:   Assay to use if `variable_type` is `"feature"`.

`layer`

:   Seurat expression layer to use for features (default `"counts"`).

`images`

:   Names of the Seurat images to use.

`image_scale`

:   Image scale for `SeuratObject::GetTissueCoordinates()`. If `NULL`, the function uses the value stored in the SIRUP object.

`swap_coords`

:   Swap the two Seurat coordinate axes? If `NULL`, the function uses the value stored in the SIRUP object. Give a value if `object` is a Seurat object.

`radius`

:   Distance that defines a neighborhood. If `NULL`, the function uses the `k` nearest neighbors.

`k`

:   Number of nearest neighbors, used if `radius` is `NULL` (default 6).

`slot`

:   Name of the receptor slot to use. Leave it `NULL` if the SIRUP object has one receptor table. You must give it if the object has several slots and the function reads receptors. The function ignores `slot` if you give a plain receptor table.

## Details

The function builds one neighbor graph from all spots, with `radius` or `k` as in [`spatialMoran()`](spatialMoran.md). Set `variable_type = "clone"` to use a 0/1 value for each spot: 1 if the spot contains the clone, 0 if not.

If the data come from more than one image, or a sirup object with multiple samples, then the function builds one graph and runs one test for each sample or image.

## Value

A data frame with the coordinates, the values, local Moran\'s I, the z-scores, and the p-values.

## See Also

[`plotSpatialLocalMoran()`](plotSpatialLocalMoran.md), [`spatialMoran()`](spatialMoran.md)

## Examples

``` R
x <- readSIRUP(system.file("extdata", "sirup_synthetic.rds", package = "SIRUP"))
local_moran <- spatialLocalMoran(x, "gene1", k = 4)
head(local_moran[, c("cell", "local_i", "z_i", "p_value")])
```

functions.title: Calculate global Moran's I
functions.summary: `spatialMoran` tests one variable for spatial autocorrelation across spots using Moran\'s I.
functions.markdown:
# spatialMoran

## Calculate global Moran\'s I

## Description

`spatialMoran` tests one variable for spatial autocorrelation across spots using Moran\'s I.

## Usage

``` R
spatialMoran(
  object,
  variable,
  variable_type = c("feature", "metadata", "receptor", "clone"),
  value = NULL,
  receptors = NULL,
  spatial_id = NULL,
  clone = NULL,
  assay = NULL,
  layer = "counts",
  images = NULL,
  image_scale = NULL,
  swap_coords = NULL,
  radius = NULL,
  k = 6,
  alternative = "greater",
  slot = NULL
)
```

## Arguments

`object`

:   Seurat object or SIRUP object.

`variable`

:   Name of the feature or the metadata column to test.

`variable_type`

:   Type of `variable`: `feature` (gene expression), `metadata` (Seurat metadata column), `receptor` (receptor table column), or `clone` (clone ID).

`value`

:   Metadata value to convert to a 0/1 indicator (default `NULL`).

`receptors`

:   AIRR-style receptor table. You must give it if `variable_type` is `"receptor"` or `"clone"` and `object` is not a SIRUP object.

`spatial_id`

:   Name of the `receptors` column that holds the spatial IDs. If `object` is a SIRUP object and this argument is `NULL`, the function uses the stored spatial ID field. Give a value if you use separate Seurat and receptor objects.

`clone`

:   Name of the `receptors` column that holds the clone IDs. The function uses it only if `variable_type` is `"clone"`. If `object` is a SIRUP object and this argument is `NULL`, the function uses the stored clone field, if there is one.

`assay`

:   Assay to use if `variable_type` is `"feature"`.

`layer`

:   Seurat expression layer to use for features (default `"counts"`).

`images`

:   Names of the Seurat images to use.

`image_scale`

:   Image scale for `SeuratObject::GetTissueCoordinates()`. If `NULL`, the function uses the value stored in the SIRUP object.

`swap_coords`

:   Swap the two Seurat coordinate axes? If `NULL`, the function uses the value stored in the SIRUP object. Give a value if `object` is a Seurat object.

`radius`

:   Distance that defines a neighborhood. If `NULL`, the function uses `k`.

`k`

:   Number of nearest neighbors, used if `radius` is `NULL` (default 6).

`alternative`

:   Alternative hypothesis for `spdep::moran.test()` (default `"greater"`).

`slot`

:   Name of the receptor slot to use. Leave it `NULL` if the SIRUP object has one receptor table. You must give it if the object has several slots and the function reads receptors. The function ignores `slot` if you give a plain receptor table.

## Details

The function builds a neighbor graph from the spot coordinates. It uses all spots within `radius`. If `radius` is `NULL`, it uses the `k` nearest spots (or fewer, if the image has fewer spots). Then it calls `spdep::moran.test()` on the variable values. The function drops spots with non-finite values.

If the data come from more than one image, or a sirup object with multiple samples, then the function builds one graph and runs one test for each sample or image.

Set `variable_type = "clone"` to test where one clone occurs. The function makes a 0/1 value for each spot: 1 if sthe spot contains the clone, 0 if not.

## Value

For one image, a list with these items: `test` (the `spdep::moran.test()` result), `data` (the values tested), `neighbors` and `weights` (from `spdep`), `radius`, `k`, and `variable`. For several images, the list has `tests`, `neighbors`, and `weights` as named lists with one entry for each image. It also has `summary`, a data frame with one row for each image (`image`, `statistic`, `p_value`, `moran_i`, `expectation`, `variance`), and the items `data`, `radius`, `k`, and `variable`.

## See Also

[`spatialLocalMoran()`](spatialLocalMoran.md), [`spatialLee()`](spatialLee.md), [`spatialCloneJoinCount()`](spatialCloneJoinCount.md)

## Examples

``` R
x <- readSIRUP(system.file("extdata", "sirup_synthetic.rds", package = "SIRUP"))

# Test gene1 for spatial autocorrelation.
result <- spatialMoran(x, "gene1", k = 4)
result$test
```

functions.title: Calculate Ripley's cross K
functions.summary: `spatialRipleyCrossK` measures how spots of mark `i` cluster around spots of mark `j` at different distances.
functions.markdown:
# spatialRipleyCrossK

## Calculate Ripley\'s cross K

## Description

`spatialRipleyCrossK` measures how spots of mark `i` cluster around spots of mark `j` at different distances. Similar to Lee\'s L but better for factor data.

## Usage

``` R
spatialRipleyCrossK(
  object,
  mark_col,
  i,
  j,
  nsim = 0,
  max_r = NULL,
  r = NULL,
  image_scale = NULL,
  swap_coords = NULL
)
```

## Arguments

`object`

:   Seurat object or SIRUP object.

`mark_col`

:   Name of the metadata column that holds the point types.

`i`

:   First mark level.

`j`

:   Second mark level.

`nsim`

:   Number of random-label simulations for the envelope (default 0). Use `0` for the observed K only.

`max_r`

:   Largest radius to calculate. The function ignores it if you give `r`.

`r`

:   Vector of distances for `spatstat.explore::Kcross()`.

`image_scale`

:   Image scale for `SeuratObject::GetTissueCoordinates()`. If `NULL`, the function uses the value stored in the SIRUP object.

`swap_coords`

:   Swap the two Seurat coordinate axes? If `NULL`, the function uses the value stored in the SIRUP object. Give a value if `object` is a Seurat object.

## Details

The function calls `spatstat.explore::Kcross()` with the border correction. If `nsim` is greater than 0, it also builds an envelope from random label simulations.

If the data come from more than one image, or a sirup object with multiple samples, then the function builds one graph and runs one test for each sample or image.

## Value

A list with these items: `observed` (the observed K), `envelope` (the simulation envelope, if any), `plot_data`, `points` (the point data), `i`, `j`, `correction`, `nsim`, `max_r`, and `r`.

## See Also

[`plotRipleyCrossK()`](plotRipleyCrossK.md)

## Examples

``` R

x <- readSIRUP(system.file("extdata", "sirup_synthetic.rds", package = "SIRUP"))

# Compare spots of type A with spots of type B. Use 19 random-label
# simulations for the envelope.
set.seed(1)
kcross <- spatialRipleyCrossK(
  x,
  mark_col = "cell_type",
  i = "A",
  j = "B",
  nsim = 19
)
head(kcross$plot_data)
```

# subsetSIRUP

## Subset a SIRUP object

## Description

`subsetSIRUP` keeps selected samples, spatial IDs, and receptor rows of a SIRUP object. `filterSample` keeps only the samples you name.

## Usage

``` R
subsetSIRUP(
  x,
  sample_id = NULL,

  receptor_rows = NULL,

  validate = TRUE
)

filterSample(x, sample_id, keep_analyses = FALSE, validate = TRUE)
```

## Arguments

`x`

:   A SIRUP object.

`sample_id`

:   Name or names of the spatial samples to keep. Use it only if the object holds a named list of Seurat objects.

`spatial_id`

:   Spatial IDs (barcodes) to keep. In a multi-sample object, the function matches the IDs in each selected sample.

`receptor_rows`

:   Logical vector with length `nrow(getReceptors(x, slot = slot))`, or a function. The function takes the receptor tibble of `slot` and returns such a vector. The function keeps the rows where the vector is `TRUE`. It applies this filter to `slot` only. The other filters apply to every slot.

`slot`

:   Name of the receptor slot that `receptor_rows` applies to. Leave it `NULL` if the object has one receptor table. You must give it if the object has several slots and you use `receptor_rows`.

`keep_nonspatial_receptors`

:   Keep receptor rows that have no spatial ID after the other filters (default `FALSE`)? The function uses this argument only if you give `spatial_id`.

`keep_analyses`

:   Keep the stored analyses (default `FALSE`)? Most analyses depend on the original spatial and receptor data.

`drop_empty_spatial`

:   Drop samples that have no cells left after the `spatial_id` filter (default `TRUE`)? The function uses this argument only for multi-sample objects.

`validate`

:   Validate the subset object (default `TRUE`)?

## Details

The function subsets the Seurat data, the receptor rows, the stored polygons, and the analyses. It applies the stored polygons again to the subset, so the polygon columns stay consistent.

## Value

A SIRUP object that contains the subset.

## See Also

[`mergeSIRUP()`](mergeSIRUP.md), [`createSIRUP()`](createSIRUP.md)

## Examples

``` R
x <- readSIRUP(system.file("extdata", "sirup_synthetic.rds", package = "SIRUP"))

# Keep three spots.
subsetSIRUP(x, spatial_id = c("spot01", "spot02", "spot03"))

# Keep the receptor rows of clone 2.
subsetSIRUP(x, receptor_rows = function(receptors) receptors$clone_id == "2")

# Keep one sample of a multi-sample object.
merged <- mergeSIRUP(x, x, samples = c("a", "b"))
filterSample(merged, "a")
```

functions.title: Summarize polygon diversity at one value of q
functions.summary: `summarizePolygonDiversity` takes the diversity estimate for one diversity order q from a stored analysis.
functions.markdown:
# summarizePolygonDiversity

## Summarize polygon diversity at one value of q

## Description

`summarizePolygonDiversity` takes the diversity estimate for one diversity order q from a stored analysis. It makes one table row for each polygon and stores the table as a new analysis.

## Usage

``` R
summarizePolygonDiversity(
  object,
  q,
  diversity_analysis = NULL,
  analysis_name = NULL,
  tolerance = sqrt(.Machine$double.eps),
  slot = NULL,
  validate = TRUE
)
```

## Arguments

`object`

:   SIRUP object.

`q`

:   Diversity order to take, for example `2` for Simpson diversity.

`diversity_analysis`

:   Name of the stored analysis from [`polygonDiversity()`](polygonDiversity.md). If `NULL`, the function uses `"polygon_diversity"`, or `"polygon_diversity_<slot>"` if the object has several receptor slots.

`analysis_name`

:   Name for the stored table. If `NULL`, the function uses `polygon_diversity_q` followed by the value of `q`, and the slot name if the object has several receptor slots.

`tolerance`

:   Tolerance for the match of `q` (default `sqrt(.Machine$double.eps)`).

`slot`

:   Name of the receptor slot whose diversity you summarize. The function uses it only to find the default analysis names. Leave it `NULL` if the object has one receptor table. You must give it if the object has several slots and you use the default names.

`validate`

:   Validate the updated SIRUP object (default `TRUE`)?

## Details

Polygons that [`polygonDiversity()`](polygonDiversity.md) left out, because they had fewer than `min_n` receptors, get a row with `NA` values. [`plotSpatialPolygons()`](plotSpatialPolygons.md) draws these polygons in grey. The function reads both kinds of result: one `DiversityCurve` for all polygons, and the list that `polygonDiversity(common_size = FALSE)` makes.

## Value

The updated SIRUP object, with the diversity summary as an analysis.

## See Also

[`polygonDiversity()`](polygonDiversity.md)

## Examples

``` R
x <- readSIRUP(system.file("extdata", "sirup_synthetic.rds", package = "SIRUP"))
x <- polygonDiversity(x, min_n = 2, max_q = 2, step_q = 1)
x <- summarizePolygonDiversity(x, q = 1)
listAnalyses(x)
```

functions.title: Calculate patristic distances between tips in a tree
functions.summary: `tipPatristicMatrix` returns the matrix of patristic distances between the selected tips of a tree.
functions.markdown:
# tipPatristicMatrix

## Calculate patristic distances between tips in a tree

## Description

`tipPatristicMatrix` returns the matrix of patristic distances between the selected tips of a tree. The rows and columns follow the order of `tip_labels`.

## Usage

``` R
tipPatristicMatrix(tree, tip_labels)
```

## Arguments

`tree`

:   Phylogenetic tree with the fields `edge`, `edge.length`, and `tip.label`.

`tip_labels`

:   Character vector of the tip labels to use.

## Value

A numeric matrix of patristic distances.

## See Also

[`clusterTreeTips()`](clusterTreeTips.md)

## Examples

``` R
x <- readSIRUP(system.file("extdata", "sirup_synthetic.rds", package = "SIRUP"))
x <- formatSpatialClones(
  x,
  id = "sequence_id",
  germ = "germline_alignment_d_mask",
  traits = "spatial_id"
)
x <- getSpatialTrees(x)
trees <- getAnalysis(x, "trees")
tree <- trees$trees[[1]]

tipPatristicMatrix(tree, tree$tip.label[1:4])
```

functions.title: Validate a SIRUP object
functions.summary: `validateSIRUP` checks that the parts of a SIRUP object agree with each other.
functions.markdown:
# validateSIRUP

## Validate a SIRUP object

## Description

`validateSIRUP` checks that the parts of a SIRUP object agree with each other.

## Usage

``` R
validateSIRUP(x, verbose = FALSE)
```

## Arguments

`x`

:   Object to validate.

`verbose`

:   Print a short summary of the result (default `FALSE`)?

## Details

The function gives an error if one of these checks fails:

- The object does not have class `sirup`.

- No receptor spatial ID matches a cell or spot name in the Seurat object. The function checks every receptor slot.

- A column named in `metadata$receptor_fields` does not exist in the receptor table. The `spatial_id` column must be in every receptor slot. Each other named column, such as `clone_id`, must be in at least one slot.

- The `sample` field is set, but the column is missing from a receptor table or from the Seurat metadata.

An object with several receptor slots can have a slot with no rows. For example, one section can have BCRs and no TCRs. The function skips the spatial ID checks for that slot.

## Value

`x`, invisibly, if the object is valid. If not, the function gives an error.

## See Also

[`createSIRUP()`](createSIRUP.md), [`isSIRUP()`](isSIRUP.md)

## Examples

``` R
x <- readSIRUP(system.file("extdata", "sirup_synthetic.rds", package = "SIRUP"))
validateSIRUP(x)
validateSIRUP(x, verbose = TRUE)
```

functions.title: Apply a function to the receptors of each polygon
functions.summary: `withPolygons` splits the receptor table by polygon and applies a function to the rows of each polygon.
functions.markdown:
# withPolygons

## Apply a function to the receptors of each polygon

## Description

`withPolygons` splits the receptor table by polygon and applies a function to the rows of each polygon. Or it applies the function once to all receptors in any polygon.

## Usage

``` R
withPolygons(
  receptors,
  .f,
  ...,
  polygons = NULL,
  polygon_id = "polygon",
  mode = c("by_polygon", "all_polygons"),
  pass_polygon_id = FALSE,
  slot = NULL
)
```

## Arguments

`receptors`

:   SIRUP object, or an AIRR-style receptor table.

`.f`

:   Function to apply.

`...`

:   Other arguments for `.f`.

`polygons`

:   Polygon table that sets the order of the output polygons. If `NULL`, the function takes the polygon IDs from the SIRUP object, or from the `polygon_id` values in `receptors`.

`polygon_id`

:   Name of the column that holds the primary polygon of each receptor (default `"polygon"`).

`mode`

:   `"by_polygon"` runs `.f` once for each polygon. `"all_polygons"` runs `.f` once on all receptors in any polygon.

`pass_polygon_id`

:   Pass the current polygon ID to `.f` as the argument `polygon_id`, if `.f` accepts it (default `FALSE`)?

`slot`

:   Name of the receptor slot to use. Leave it `NULL` if the SIRUP object has one receptor table. You must give it if the object has several slots. The function ignores `slot` if you give a plain receptor table.

## Value

For `mode = "by_polygon"`, a named list with one result for each polygon. Otherwise, the result of `.f`.

## See Also

[`assignReceptorPolygons()`](assignReceptorPolygons.md), [`polygonAbundance()`](polygonAbundance.md), [`polygonDiversity()`](polygonDiversity.md)

## Examples

``` R
x <- readSIRUP(system.file("extdata", "sirup_synthetic.rds", package = "SIRUP"))

# Count the receptors in each polygon.
withPolygons(x, nrow)

# Count the receptors in all polygons together.
withPolygons(x, nrow, mode = "all_polygons")
```

functions.title: Write sequences to a FASTQ or FASTA file
functions.summary: `writeFastqas` writes a table of sequences to a FASTQ or FASTA file.
functions.markdown:
# writeFastqas

## Write sequences to a FASTQ or FASTA file

## Description

`writeFastqas` writes a table of sequences to a FASTQ or FASTA file.

## Usage

``` R
writeFastqas(
  df,
  fn,
  type = "fq",
  header_col = "id",
  append = FALSE,
  nthreads = 1
)
```

## Arguments

`df`

:   Data frame or data.table with a `seq` column. For FASTQ, it also needs a `qual` column. The `header_col` column holds the record headers.

`fn`

:   Path of the output file.

`type`

:   File type: `"fq"` (default), `"fastq"`, `"fa"`, or `"fasta"`.

`header_col`

:   Name of the column that holds the record headers (default `"id"`). Use `"full_id"` to write the full header.

`append`

:   Add the records to an existing file (default `FALSE`)?

`nthreads`

:   Number of threads for `data.table::fwrite()` (default 1).

## Value

`fn`, invisibly.

## See Also

[`processSpatialSample()`](processSpatialSample.md)

## Examples

``` R
reads <- data.frame(id = c("read1", "read2"), seq = c("ACGTACGT", "TTGACCGA"))
path <- tempfile(fileext = ".fasta")
writeFastqas(reads, path, type = "fasta")
readLines(path)
```
